speechtext: The House resumed from Thursday, January 24, consideration of the motion of Mr. Stevens that Bill C-15, and Act respecting investment in Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Regional Development.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique Tardif (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Bill now before the House is a major piece of legislation. It provides the cornerstone for a very substantial part of our economy. Bill C-15 should be seen as a dynamic measure to promote and welcome the positive contribution that can be made by foreign investment, since the specific mandate of Investment Canada is to encourage investment in order to promote growth and increase employment. By being positive with investors and providing them with a good environment, not only will Canadian businesses remain in business, they will expand and hire more employees. However, to make this happen, it must be made clear that Canada is open for business. That is what Investment Canada wants to do, and it is vital to our economy.
In fact, I know very few business people who would want to invest in a plant that is apparently closing down. We must make it abundantly clear that we are in business for good and that investment is welcome. That is how we intend to keep Canada, this beautiful country of ours, from being sold for a song to foreign interests.
Mr. Speaker, people buy an old warehouse to tear it down, but they invest their money in a business that is doing well. We must revamp our economic image for the rest of the world. We must do what too many years of Liberal neglect have left undone, and that is exactly what this Bill intends to do.
Mr. Speaker, it is most unfortunate that despite the very real importance of the Bill now before the House, the quality of the debate on this legislation should be so poor. Up to now, more than fourteen hours of debate have been spent on Bill C-15. Thirty-one Liberals, 25 New Democratic Party Members and 13 of my own colleagues have taken the floor. Mr. Speaker, my point is that at this stage, the debate is lagging and languishing. The Opposition is repeating the same arguments over and over again. They are saying we want to sell out Canada at any price and that our country is going to become the fifty-first State. We have explained very clearly that the Bill contains the necessary guarantees that it will welcome foreign investors and stimulate Canadian investment while at the same time preserving our national identity.
They say it will create unemployment at a later stage. We have described the positive impact of the creation of new jobs and reduction of unemployment in the short term. I would think jobs are what Canada really needs now.
On the issue of research and development, they complain that Canada will not have its share. We have answered time and time again that although the legislation is not directly concerned with promoting research and development-the Government has other policies to that effect-the direct impact of clauses 5 and 20(c) will be to promote research and development in Canada.
The Liberals accuse us of breaking with a tradition established by Sir John A. Macdonald, a tradition that supported protectionism, especially where the United States was concerned. I would say that the Official Opposition, which today is taking an anti-American protectionist line, is the one that is breaking with a traditional position of its Party, a tradition adhered to more specifically by one of their leaders, Mackenzie King, who was Prime Minister in the 20th century, not the 19th century. Times have changed, Mr. Speaker, though not everyone seems to realize it.
Finally, and this was a real stroke of genius, they accused us last week of breaking our election promises and refusing to listen to the outcome of the consultations on this Bill. Mr. Speaker, there has been considerable proof to the contrary. First of all, from what we have been able to gather in our ridings and from letters from constituents, we can conclude, and they know it, that the majority of Canadians are in favour of the measures proposed in Bill C-15. In fact, I think the best way to prove this would be to immediately refer the Bill to committee where witnesses and intervenors can be heard.
Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that the Liberal and New Democratic Party Members will support this motion if they are truly concerned, as they claimed last week they were, about helping us fulfil our election promises.
As one of their own, the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) said, the real work on a Bill does not take place

January 28, 1985
Investment Canada Act
in the House. Let us therefore proceed and go to committee right away.
Mr. Speaker, at this stage in the debate, the Opposition has exhausted its arguments but continues to take the floor, one Member after another. It is clear from the repetitiveness of the Opposition's arguments and the fact that they have nothing more to say about the Bill. I may refer to the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker), who, quite candidly, set the tone for the debate as the first Member to take the floor when the House reconvened last Monday. In concluding his speech, he said, and I quote:
1 have not even been able to address the Bill since I began speaking at eleven o'clock.
That says it all, Mr. Speaker. Especially since we have had 56 speeches from the Opposition's 70 Members. It seems to me they cannot complain we are preventing them from speaking to this Bill.
Instead of wasting our allotted time, I suggest that we proceed immediately with the next stage. Canadians will thank us for doing so. If we do not know how to manage our time, how can we manage the country?
Mr. Speaker, I therefore move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine):
That the question now be put.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. It may well be that I have misunderstood the rules and perhaps you could help me in this regard. However, it was my understanding that it required a Minister of the Crown to move such a motion. Perhaps you could clarify that for me, Mr. Speaker. I seem to recall that as being the case.

Perhaps the Hon. Member would like to find the rule in the Standing Orders that makes such a stipulation. All I find is Standing Order 56 which simply indicates that once the motion is put, it precludes all other amendments. That is all Standing Order 56 indicates. I am prepared to hear argument on the matter if the Hon. Member has some argument to make. However, I know of no such argument that would have its foundation in our Standing Orders.

Mr. Speaker, quite frankly, I was caught a little by surprise by the putting of the motion. I would have anticipated its having been put by a Minister. I assume you would allow me to make some argument on the matter after Question Period today in the event I am able between now and then to come up with what I believe to be the situation, which is that it would require a Minister to move such a motion. I would simply ask that you allow me the latitude of making such argument should I wish to after Question Period today.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on the same point of order. The step taken by the Hon. Member is one that comes
with some surprise and disappointment to members of that caucus because, as we all know, this Bill is a centrepiece of the entire economic strategy of the Government. Therefore, one would have thought that a member of the Ministry would have been responsible for the drastic action that has now been proposed. As a result, I think the motion should be held in abeyance until such time as we can marshal those arguments, because I think it is a very curious, strange and somewhat unorthodox move to have a Member of the Commons move this motion and to have Ministers of the Crown absolve themselves of all responsibility for such a diabolical and difficult initiative which closes off debate on such an important Bill.

I am in some difficulty. I must say to Hon. Members that I cannot reserve on this matter. As a matter of public record, the last time this motion was moved was under the previous Government and it was moved by a Private Member on the back-bench. There is a clear procedural paper out on this matter for all Members to follow and there is no question in my mind from reading the rules that there is no restriction on the moving of this motion in terms of whether it be by a Minister of the Crown, a Parliamentary Secretary, or a Private Member.
In fact, as Hon. Members may know, the motion is usable during Private Members' Hour, which means by definition that it must be moveable by a Private Member. Therefore, I find that I have no reason to reserve and that the motion is properly before the House. For the record, as I am reminded, the motion is, of course, debatable. Debate.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak on the motion which was moved by the Hon. Member for Charlesbourg (Mrs. Tardif). I suppose it is only fitting that I speak to the motion, as the Hon. Member referred to me as having spoken for 20 minutes in the previous debate and remarked that at the end of that time I had not dealt with the subject matter of the Bill. In getting myself out of that quandary, I checked and discovered that the actual motion which we were debating was a motion for a six-month hoist. The reason for that motion was that the Government had not displayed in its policy, and had not shown in its legislation, that it was consistent with its stated purpose in bringing in the legislation.
The Hon. Member stated that all of the arguments had been presented, that the Opposition was holding up the Bill, and that there was nothing new to say on the subject. I am sure all Hon. Members of this House read Hansard. We can review Hansard to see some of the excellent speeches which were given, for example the speech which was given by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy). That was one of the best speeches given this session on the Bill. One of the worst speeches was the speech of the Minister when he introduced the legislation. A very interesting speech was given by a member of the New Democratic Party; however he was continually interrupted by the Minister during his address.
January 28, 1985

In reaching my point, I would like to read into the record what the Minister said during his address to the House. He said:
I remind him that when FIRA was put in place unemployment in the country was slightly over 5 per cent. Today it is over 11 per cent.
The Minister made these remarks on December 11, 1984. He went on to say, as reported at page 1094 of Hansard:
That did not regain what we lost in 1981 and 1982. What about the money that left?
Presumably, the Minister was talking about the money which left the country. Later on in the debate the Minister disbelieved the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Lang-don) when the Member pointed out that direct foreign investment in Canada was not as the Minister claimed, and that it had actually increased over the years since FIRA had been established. The Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor stated at page 1100 of Hansard:
From a negative balance of S4.4 billion in 1981 we had a negative $900 million in 1982. In 1983 we were up to a positive $200 million and so far in 1984 we were up to a positive $1.3 billion.
Another Hon. Member in the House then asked: "What is your source?" The Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor said that his source was Statistics Canada. Of course, the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor was absolutely correct in the figures which he read into the record. What has been missed in the debate up to this point was why there was such an outflow of capital from Canada into the United States in 1981 and 1982. Was it really an outflow of cash?
If we look at the gross inflows of capital into Canada from the United States, we see that since FIRA was established in 1974 the gross inflows of capital from the United States had actually increased. The figure increased and reached its maximum in 1981. If we examine the gross outflows of investment capital from Canada into the United States, we find that that figure also peaked in 1981.
If we were to use the logic of the Minister in making the statements he did in his speech, as well as the logic used by Hon. Members in being questioned after their speeches, we could say that FIRA itself, since it was created, actually brought investment capital into Canada from the United States the like of which had never been seen before 1974. But that would be a bit dishonest. We could say as well, as the Minister claimed, that the gross outflow of capital from Canada into the United States which peaked in 1981 and 1982 was a loss to Canada, that we lost jobs in Canada because that money flowed into the United States. But the point of my argument, Mr. Speaker, is that when we examine cash outflows from any country, we have to look in effect at where that money went and for what purpose.
The fact is that Statistics Canada makes no distinction in their figures. When we examine the record and other figures we discover that that large investment in 1981 and 1982 went into buying branch plants in Canada which were owned by
Investment Canada Act
Americans. So the statistics showed really a net outflow from Canada for the years 1981 and 1982.
When we examine the figures for the United States, we would say that there was an incredible increase in the actual gross inflows into Canada from the United States from the point at which FIRA came into operation until 1981 and it still maintained a high level up to 1984. But we would also have to ask ourselves the question: What is the net U.S. direct investment? The Minister, when introducing the legislation, was very quick to point out that in 1981 and 1982 the net U.S. direct investment was a negative figure.
However, he failed to point out that there are two distinctions. The first is where that capital went. That capital went to buy branch plants located in Canada. The investment was made by Canadians but the money went to the United States. The Minister also did not point out that the largest growth in investment capital inflows into Canada from the United States happened since FIRA came into operation in 1974.
It is also interesting to note, Mr. Speaker, that in introducing her motion the Hon. Member claimed that the Progressive Conservative Government was on the way and that jobs were already created in the private sector. That, Mr. Speaker, is like the argument used by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald). But when did the greatest increase in private sector jobs happen? The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that it works out that in the three and a half months under this Government, 27,000 jobs per month were created. During the last three months of the Trudeau administration, 32,000 jobs a month were created in the private sector. During the Turner administration, 33,000 jobs per month were created in the private sector. No one, Mr. Speaker, goes back to find out how many jobs were created in the past. They use the figures with some kind of twisted logic to make it seem as if the Government is actually doing something.
By the same token, if we examine foreign investment in Canada from the United States and we match up the gross inflows with the gross outflows and come up with the net U.S. direct investment, we find that the largest amount of net investment which has come into Canada was during the first nine months of 1984. If you break it down further, by the month, you discover the greatest U.S. net direct investment came during the administration of the Turner Government. But to say that that was because of the actions of a government is really stretching the truth.
There were a lot of things missed in the debate so far on this particular legislation, Mr. Speaker, which should be brought before this House. For example, there was no comparison made of the impact of this legislation. There is a question to be asked-is my time running out, Mr. Speaker?

January 28, 1985
Investment Canada Act
I have not even gotten to the argument I wanted to present. However, I am sure there will be another opportunity to do that later in this session.

Mr. Speaker, the Government did not accept the opportunity put before it to take another six months and look at this whole area of foreign investment. This morning the Government effectively put closure on debate. That, I guess, is an indication of the kind of democracy we can expect from the 211 members of the Conservative Party who are Members of the House of Commons. They will not accept the idea of democracy being an opportunity for the Opposition to put all of its arguments before the House, as well as an opportunity for the people of Canada to see what their position is and where they are going. What the Government is now doing is limiting the amount of information which will go out to the people. It therefore becomes our responsibility to do it more directly.
One of the things which has not been brought before this House is the alternative the Government has in this whole area of foreign investment. There is no shortage of investment capital in Canada. In 1974 10 per cent of the country's gross income was put into savings. Between 1974 and 1982 it went from 10 per cent to almost 14 per cent, and it is my understanding that in 1984 and 1985 it increased further. As I said, there is lots of investment capital in Canada and we do not need to bring in foreign capital with no strings attached. The problem is an unwillingness on the part of business to invest in Canada. In light of that, the Government should be attempting to stimulate the economy so Canadians will invest. That should be the first step.
How can the Government do that? First of all, a point which has been made several times in this debate is that takeover investment is not good investment for Canada. We know foreign investment is not good investment for Canada and takeover investment has a tendency to eliminate jobs. Buying a new firm with available money does not create jobs because those jobs are already there. That is just using available capital to increase the portfolio of a particular company. Foreign capital is always suspect because it may help Canada in the beginning but at some time in the future that money is going to go back to its parent company and will not help Canada.
In some ways FIRA was not a very good operation. It did not work particularly well, but at least it was in place to define the parameters under which foreign investment could enter Canada. This Bill is attempting to take away those parameters which foreign corporations investing in Canada had to consider. Instead of allowing foreign capital to come in with no strings attached, we should be establishing criteria for the investment that is coming into Canada. After those criteria have been established, we should set up a monitoring agency. That is what FIRA was supposed to do. It did not do that well but it was there. We should be strengthening the monitoring
powers of the corporation rather than eliminating them entirely.
What should the criteria for Canadian investment be? Since our biggest problem is unemployment, investment should be aimed at that. Takeover investment should be eliminated. The impact on the local community should be included in the criteria. The amount of effective development of skills which will make long-term jobs worthwhile and increase the standard of living of the affected people should be considered. The impact of investments on the balance of payments of the country should be controlled. The eventual impact of foreign investment is to increase the flow of money out of Canada. This adversely affects our balance of payments and forces us to increase interest rates to keep the money in Canada. The criteria should also take into consideration the social impact of the investment on the community and the country.
After establishing the criteria we should establish the objectives of investment. If the Government is going to have an effect on investment and the economy, part of its expenditures must be aimed at stimulating the economy. If business is unwilling and incapable of expanding, as seems to have happened in the last few years, both federal and provincial Governments should inject investment money into the economy to stimulate it. I could name a dozen or so areas that they should be investing in. We have plenty of resources and two million unemployed. We have a great need for housing. We have lots of lumber and other products necessary for the construction industry. We have many unemployed construction workers. Therefore, the Government should stimulate housing programs to help the economy.
Public expenditures in public transit, medical care facilities and education would help stimulate the economy. I find it very disturbing that in communities with several thousand people unemployed every teacher is teaching 30, 40 or even 50 students.
The tragedy of this closure motion to limit debate is that all of these points should be put before the people of Canada as well as the Government. We should eliminate cuts in public spending which affect people directly. We should lower interest rates. All of these are good ways to stimulate the economy which have not been put before the Government. We have not asked the Government to reply to those kinds of alternatives. Instead of that, closure has been moved in order to limit this debate.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I regret that the Hon. Member's time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, I regret very much having to rise to speak on the motion which has just been put which will prevent the House from giving this very important legislation the amount of consideration which it requires. Perhaps I could take a moment to deal with the procedural aspects of the motion.
By moving the motion which has just been put, the Government is attempting to prevent members of the Opposition from moving any other substantive motions that are appropriate at
January 28, 1985

the time of second reading. Since the size of the Opposition is much smaller now than it was in some past Parliaments, this means that Parliament will be forced to vote on this legislation very shortly for the purpose of sending it on through the parliamentary process. That is an unprecedented activity and gesture by the Government in relation to the importance of these issues and the limited amount of time that has already been spent on this subject.
This legislation has only been before us since December. It has not been debated for very long in this House. It has not received too much attention in the country. Its name suggests that it does deal in one way or another with foreign investment. Foreign investment is one of the historically significant issues in Canadian public policy formation. The Government should not be attempting to get this Bill through before it comes to the attention of the vast majority of the Canadian people. The Government is attempting to prevent the Canadian public from finding out that very important changes are being made in the fundamental laws that protect the Canadian economy from the negative effects of foreign investment.
When I heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announce that Canada was open for business, I was worried. It concerned me that by that he must have meant that the foreign investment rules in the country were going to be changed in some significant ways. I am not fully certain, and I do not think anyone who has studied the legislation is, what kind of basis there will be in the future, if any, for protecting Canada from the negative impact of foreign investment.
It is important to note that under the existing legislation which was introduced by the former Liberal Government, with which we have lived since the early 1970s, there was some basis, not for excluding foreign investment from Canada because that was never the goal of the former Government and is not the wish of the Canadian people, but for assuring that foreign investment coming into our country enters on the best possible terms for Canadian interests.
It is wrong to assume that foreign investment or any investment will be good investment. Those of us who practise law and have advised foreign interests from time to time are aware that they like to preserve a certain flexibility and not be bound to the commitment of creating jobs, providing research and development, investing a certain amount of capital and to assuring that the local service sector and its related professions will be used rather than the corresponding industries in the home country of their head office. They would prefer to be completely unfettered and be taken at good faith that they will operate in the Canadian interest. While many foreign investors intend and want to do so, unless we obtain the assurance that they will make their good faith concrete, it is possible that the maximum Canadian benefit will not be attained by that foreign investor in Canada. Therefore, the process that the foreign investment review legislation contemplated was very valuable to the enhancement and development of the Canadian economy and Canadian interests.
Investment Canada Act
I am sure that all of us, even those who oppose any government role in relation to foreign investment, would like to see a Canadian economy that operates fully in the Canadian interest and that is autonomous and indigenous to the Canadian people. Although FIRA has been in effect for approximately a decade, our present economy is far from autonomous because when we First introduced policies to deal with foreign investment in Canada our economy was very much foreign controlled and foreign owned.
The very important Watkins report which was commissioned and delivered to my colleague, the Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), when he was the Minister responsible, revealed the tremendous extent to which we were not in charge of our own economy. While we were achieving considerable benefits from foreign investment, we were also subject to considerable disadvantages which that foreign investment implied.
The question was how we should go about making our economy more autonomous and encouraging the Canadianiza-tion of it in a way that would continue to allow foreign investment to come and stay in Canada. At the same time that policy would have to assure that our Canadian economy would be Canadian-managed, owned and directed to the maximum extent possible.
At the time I recall spending much of my energy Fighting for this legislation and explaining it to those who believe that the least government is the best government. I know there are still many members of the Conservative caucus and Cabinet who retain that unreconstructed Conservative attitude that does not recognize that government be a positive player and that the whole history of developing the Canadian economy has been one of using government to achieve objectives that cannot or have not been achieved otherwise.
I am not saying that in any way to criticize capitalism. I believe that Canadian or foreign entrepreneurs who can be encouraged to operate businesses in areas where profits can be earned can greatly serve the public interest by doing so. However, those entrepreneurs cannot be expected to take account of many of the objectives which are not those of free enterprise as such but very much objectives that it would be in our interest to have built into our economy. The creation of jobs itself is not a direct goal of free enterprise. The direct goal of free enterprise is to create proFits, and if this can be done by reducing employment then it can be understood that businessmen will try to replace workers with machines that produce more efFiciently.
Therefore, one must ask how that concern for employment in the economy is registered and by whom. Such reflection of the goals of business and the goals of Canadians in their economy show that there is much room for government to be active and to develop policies which do not deter the expansion of businesses but encourage and require them to take account of some of the other goals that Canadians expect their economy to deliver for them.
I am certainly prepared to concede that the foreign Investment Review Agency received bad reviews and was criticized

January 28, 1985
Investment Canada Act
in some places around the world. One reason for that is that it is a very up-front type of restraint. Although many countries have constraints on foreign investment, in most cases those constraints are less obvious. Even in the United States a foreign investor must actually visit the country and begin asking questions before discovering that there are a great many restrictions on free access by foreign businesses to the American market-place, which is perhaps the most free enterprise economy in the world.
I have seen the studies that were done for Watkins and more contemporary studies that show literally dozens of constraints in the United States. For example, there are restraints under the Jones Act, the regulations of vessels in domestic commerce, the Fishing Fleet Improvement Act and the Merchant Marine Act.
I see that my time has expired. I believe I have said enough to show that there needs to be more concern than is shown by this legislation for the negative side of foreign investment.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is the House ready for the question?
Mr. Speaker, the House certainly is not ready for the question.
Yes it is.

Perhaps Hon. Members on that side of the House are ready for the question. It is sad that they should seek to limit debate in the House so early in their career as a government. We are learning that the Conservative Party operates differently in government from when it was in opposition. When in opposition, that Party espoused respect for parliamentary democracy, wanted to reform the House of Commons to give more authority to Private Members and make this place responsible for the public purse. Now that they are in office they limit debate.
This is travesty of the political process. During the election the Conservatives promised more open government. It is now closing the door on more information to Canadians with regard to investment policy. It is a sad moment for Canadians that the Government which promised so much is delivering so little.
The purpose of the Bill that the Government is supporting and at this time attempting to push down the throats of Canadians is to deregulate foreign investment. Deregulation represents the Holy Grail to the Government, a magic formula that is supposed to bring about a rejuvenation of the Canadian economy. It is an empty promise of prosperity for all. The Government has made many promises and has broken them. When it comes before the House with a piece of legislation which once again makes further promises, we have to look behind those promises. We have to ask ourselves what the Government is doing and why it is in such a hurry to push through this piece of legislation.
The aim of this legislation is to deregulate foreign investment and to give it a free hand. Another of its aims is to allow multinational companies to come into the country and do whatever they want without the representatives of the public being able to examine whether their actions are to the benefit of Canadians.
From past experience would we have any reason to want to examine what foreign investment does in Canada? Has foreign investment in the past always been so beneficial that we can assume that it would be done in the interests of Canadians? I should like to raise a couple of questions about the impact of foreign investment in Canada, questions which I think will lead to the conclusion that it is necessary to have some reasonable regulation of foreign investment.
Foreign investment has led to a Canadian economy which is largely dependent upon branch plants in the manufacturing area of the economy, like young children of parent companies in other countries. The branch plant economy in Canada is largely dependent upon its parent companies in the United States.
What happens with a branch plant economy? We are just coming out of the last recession. It is a recession in which we have not recovered from the loss of employment which Canadians are still suffering. There were massive losses of employment during that recession. One of the reasons we lost many jobs was that our economy was vulnerable to the downturn in international economic activity because of our branch plant economy. With the downturn in the economy, the branch plants returned jobs to their parent plants, largely in the United States. They let jobs go in Canada to preserve employment in the United States. It was not only a matter of individual decisions by individual companies; it was a matter of public policy in the United States. Obviously it is in the interests of the American Government to protect as much as possible the employment of its own people. How could one criticize a government which took action to protect the employment of its people?
The Government of Canada, and particularly the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), is a great admirer of the American Government and the American President. I wish the Prime Minister would learn from what that President has done in the area of investment. He has protected employment for his own people over employment in other countries. We need to learn from those actions rather than from the rhetoric of the American President. We need to understand that if we want to protect employment for Canadians, we must have appropriate government policy. We not only need activity in the private sector, we not only need entrepreneurs in Canada who have the courage to create investment and jobs; we also need appropriate government policy in order to ensure that we protect the jobs we already have and the Canadian economy. When the economy turns down and we are still based upon a branch plant economy, we tend to lose more jobs than we would lose if our economy was largely based upon Canadian enterprises.
January 28, 1985

Even when the economy picks up, as it is beginning to do now, one problem with an economy largely based upon foreign investment and therefore upon branch plants is that we do not receive the full benefit of investments or economic activity in the country. If a company produces a particular product here which can be sold in the Canadian market and buys the materials it needs to produce the product, it tends to buy the goods from its parent company in the United States. Therefore local Canadian firms, particularly small businesses, lose the market because of the way in which the economy is structured. That is crucial to employment for Canadians. We all know- even the Government knows from time to time-that the part of the economy which produces the most employment is small business. We should be doing everything we can to support small business in Canada.
I see Mr. Speaker indicating that I have only a couple of minutes remaining. One way to support small business in the country is to have an economy based upon Canadian enterprises more than branch plant enterprises, because those enterprises tend to buy more locally and support small business, which in turn creates the most employment possible.
In summary, it is sad and tragic that the Government has moved at this moment to limit debate on a Bill which seeks to deregulate foreign investment. It is a tragedy because it is important for Canadians to examine fully the impact of foreign investment in Canada. We need investment to create jobs, but we need investment which will be responsible. It is incumbent upon the Government to put in place the necessary policies to ensure responsible behaviour by investors in the country so that Canadians have secure jobs.
I ask the Government to open up debate on this question rather than close it down. I ask it to run an open government and make its first concern Canadians and their employment rather than some ideological notion that if it simply deregulates foreign investment, the economy in Canada will automatically improve. We need a serious examination of this legislation. I ask the Government to open up debate rather than close it down.

Mr. Speaker, it is regrettable that one of the first initiatives of the new Member for Charlesbourg (Mrs. Tardif)-who has changed her seat but who is in this House where I am much more at ease to speak to her-What I want to say is that it is regrettable that the new Member for Charlesbourg has decided to impose closure on such an important debate in the House. I expected a more constructive approach on the part of the Hon. Member. Her constituents will surely be quite surprised to see her impatience, I would even say her arrogance and certainly, at the very least, her lack of democratic spirit. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, one has to read Standing Order 56 to appreciate the seriousness of the initiative taken by the Member for Charlesbourg., Here is Standing Order 56:
Investment Canada Act
The previous question, until it is decided, shall preclude all amendments of the main question, and shall be in the following words, "That this question be now put".
And here is Standing Order 56(2) which I quote for the benefit of new Members in this House, especially some of the new Progressive Conservative Members who may not have had an opportunity to read and fully understand the Standing Orders:
If the previous question be resolved in the affirmative, the original question is to be put forthwith without any amendment or debate.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Charlesbourg has just moved closure this morning, nothing more, nothing less. With such an overwhelming majority, I would have thought that this government would have been very careful not to show exactly where it stands so early in this new Parliament, because what this means is that Members of the Opposition, Liberals and New Democrats alike, will no longer be able to debate this issue which, to my mind, underlies the Canadian economy. Why-and I am asking the question seriously-why did a Progressive Conservative Minister not have enough courage to do that dirty work himself? Why did they ask a backbencher to do what I call the dirty job of gagging the Opposition in the House of Commons?
I find that regrettable and unfortunate because the new younger Member seems to be quite charming, but someone has taken advantage of her naivete or perhaps her lack of parliamentary experience, and I think it must have been the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens). Where is that Minister?
Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I would point out to you that since December 11, the day he introduced this Bill, the Minister responsible for this measure has seldom been seen in the House. You used to sit with him in the Opposition and you recall how the Minister, who was then on this side of the House, would take the government and Liberal Ministers to task for showing disrespect for the Canadian Parliament. Mr. Speaker, the current Minister would never have allowed consideration of such an important piece of legislation to proceed without the regular attendance of the Minister responsible. He did show up for a few minutes in this debate, but most of the time the Minister has been away from the House, as he is now.
The Progressive Conservatives have 40 ministers, but right now I can see only two of them in the House.

speechtext: This is not a point of order. The Hon. Member should not reflect on who is in the House and who is not. I am sure the Hon. Member knows that.

Mr. Speaker, I think the Canadian public should be told that the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens), who is responsible for this legislation, is not here this morning and that he has taken virtually no part in this most important debate that can substantially alter Canada's economic outlook.
Why do we Liberals so strongly oppose this Bill? Because it is our fundamental belief that in our Canadian context we should control our economy. With this legislation, the Tories are ready to sell out at any price, to anybody, at any time, and in this debate we will fight to the limit, even though with her underhand practices this morning the Hon. Member for Char-lesbourg (Mrs. Tardif) is attempting to muzzle us. The amazing part of it is that Bill C-15 would have us approve post haste a new concept for our Canadian economy. The legislation is presented by the Tory government as a means to create new jobs. We say outright, Mr. Speaker, that this legislation is wrong, and that far from creating new jobs, it will probably mean the loss of their jobs to hundreds of Canadians.
I am pleased to note the presence in the House of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. C6te), who is responsible for competition in Canada. Since he has already been doing his homework, he is aware of the extent of large business concentration in Canada, he knows that in most major sectors of the Canadian economy there are only two or three corporations that control the Canadian economic market. Competition is exceedingly difficult to exercise in Canada, and the Canadian consumers are at the constant mercy of a few big corporations.
The first thing the Conservative Government did when coming to power was to bow to the big multinational oil corporations. We wanted to Canadianize the oil industry. We passed legislation to allow for and promote the Canadianiza-tion of that important industry, and we created Petro-Canada. But the Conservatives never accepted that. They always wanted to support the multinational corporations, those foreign corporations which control the Canadian oil industry and rip off the Canadian consumers.
I therefore say that Bill C-15 is a bad bill, because it will allow the big and the strong to meddle with the international economy and bully our small businessmen in Canada, because the Tory legislation now under consideration no longer contains the same requirements, the same important criteria as were provided in the measure we introduced in 1974, and under which the Foreign Investment Review Agency could prevail on new Canadian investors to give guarantees, not only
to create new jobs, but at least to guarantee existing jobs, and especially to promote economic growth. This legislation would allow investors a free hand. Anybody may now invest in Canada without constraints, without any obligation to Canadians. This is what we are fighting against. It is not good enough and we are sorry that the Hon. Member for Charlesbourg (Mrs. Tardif) should be attempting to use the guillotine so early in her political career. This is a bad omen indeed.

Mr. Speaker, I am very interested in contributing to this debate this morning, even though our time is limited to 10 minutes.
Before getting into the substance of my remarks, I wish to remind the House, particularly new Members, that for many years we fought very hard in this country to develop a national economy. In the 1950s this country was virtually owned by foreigners, both our natural resource industry and our manufacturing industry. When I was a younger man, and well into the 1960s, there was a great wave of nationalism spreading across the country. It was not a particularly healthy kind of nationalism. It was born out of a normal and understandable resentment which had developed, based largely on the fact that there was not only the impression in the country but the facts to back up that impression that successive Governments, particularly Liberal Governments, were selling out our country to foreign interests. That was happening in mining, smelting, the newsprint industry, the forest products industry and metal mining. It was happening in financial institutions and, primarily, in manufacturing. It created a very negative kind of thinking throughout the country. That was not healthy.
If we go ahead with Bill C-15 and set up Investment Canada, I suggest that not tomorrow or next year but in five or 10 years that unhealthy, negative nationalism will return as we see the manufacturing and resource sectors of our economy once again slipping out of our hands. I can recall a time when about 80 per cent of our natural resource industry in the country was either directly or indirectly controlled or owned outright by foreign interests. Not many years ago I can recall a time when about 60 per cent of the manufacturing sector was controlled or owned outright by foreign interests. It was not healthy.
I would like to impress upon Government Members as others already have that it is not always of benefit to sell out to a foreign company. It is not always a good thing for an American firm to buy out a Canadian firm. In fact, very often quite the opposite eventually happens. It may not happen overnight, in a few weeks or a few months, but eventually it does happen. Some of our Canadian industries become nothing more than warehouses or distribution points for goods manufactured offshore.
Foreign firms are not the best of employers. Although I do not have time in a ten-minute speech to go into it in detail, the record shows that this is so. We all know that the first companies to lay off employees in an economic recession are
January 28, 1985

the foreign-owned ones. Obviously they want to look after their own employees at their own head offices wherever those head offices may be, whether in Des Moines, Iowa, West Germany, Sweden, or Japan.
In terms of research and development, the record speaks for itself. The plants with the best record in research and development in this country are Canadian-owned plants. Yet this Bill would put heavy competitive pressure on our Canadian-owned industries and would dampen that enthusiasm and desire to do research and development here in Canada because foreign-owned companies almost always do most of their R and D offshore. These days they do it in the countries with the best tax system, the lowest tax system, usually Third World countries. Of course, there is a dog's breakfast looming on the horizon there to which we will all have to face up very quickly. If they do not do their R and D in the Third World, they do it at the parent plant which is usually in the United States. As well, large percentages of profits, bonuses, dividends and the like are sucked back into the United States by American corporations, and again this puts some downward pressure on our dollar.
I admit that not all foreign companies in this country are operated as branch plants, but many of them are. Those that are operated as branch plants are very restricted in what they can do in terms of marketing. For example, they cannot compete with the mother industry back home so they tend to have very restricted markets. They sell only to the Canadian market. After all, the reason they came here in the first place was to jump the tariff barrier. They came to Canada to get over the tariff barrier by establishing a small plant in Canada to serve a limited Canadian market.
If a foreign-owned plant is operated as a branch plant, as many of them if not the majority of them are, then it has a very restricted market. In the domestic market it is restricted to Canadian sales but it is also restricted in terms of foreign sales. Again, in many cases these firms are told not in writing but by telephone at ten o'clock every morning where they can sell, how much they can sell, and what the price will be here in Canada. They are told not to compete with the mother company overseas because the mother company already has that market nicely sewn up.
I have spoken to a few managers of branch plants in my time. They will admit, if I promise never to quote them or name their companies, that they are frustrated with their lack of manoeuverability and lack of ability to apply creative talents to improving the industry. They are always being held back by their bosses offshore wherever the parent plant happens to be.
I would like to remind members of the Conservative Government to keep something in mind when trying to sell Canada to foreign corporations and particularly to American-owned corporations. I wonder what the reaction would be in the United States if the average American who had no interest whatsoever in the economy, big business or international trade and finance was on his way to a football game and was told that that country to the north called Canada controlled over half of all
Investment Canada Act
American manufacturing and perhaps 60 per cent of its natural resource industry. The Americans are great ones for saying that they want Japanese, British, French and Canadian capital in their country. However, how many people on the other side realize what the total picture is?
Less than 3 per cent of non-financial privately-owned commercial enterprise in the United States is actually controlled or owned outright by foreigners. Here we are in Canada desperately trying to hold on to a Canadian national economy, to compete in an international market-place as freely and unfettered as possible, and this Government wants to destroy the only instrument we had to reasonably and rationally control foreign investment in the country, the Foreign Investment Review Agency, an agency which the NDP forced the Liberals to bring in under a minority government.
Those people opposite want to destroy FIRA. They are not saying "Canada is open for business"; they are saying "Canada is open for exploitation, come up here and rape us". That is what those Members are saying to the big interests in the United States, Europe and throughout the world. I think that is a shame. If we lose our national economy, we will lose our national character, ethos and culture. Those too will go down the tubes and we will simply be a white mass sitting on top of the United States.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had intended to speak on Bill C-15 this morning, but I was certainly not expecting such a surprise move. I would never have thought that the new Member for Charlesbourg (Mrs. Tardif) would come in and propose a form of closure to bring to an end this debate as quickly as possible, in spite of its importance for the economic future of Canada.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouel-let), said a while ago that the Progressive Conservative Government had called on a newly elected Member to do its dirty work and impose closure. However, I think that he made a mistake in saying that this new Member is simply a private Member, because, if I am not mistaken, she is Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens). The motion is therefore an official proposal of the Progressive Conservative Party. It is not simply a case of a backbencher making a mistake and thinking it would be a good idea to put an end to this debate. On the contrary! The Parliamentary Secretary represents her Minister quite well, and in fact, she really needs to do it because the Minister is never here during the debate. She has become the spokesperson of her party in proposing this despicable motion which reflects a Government decision and which is, I repeat, an obvious abuse, this early in this Parliament, of the enormous

January 28, 1985
Investment Canada Act
majority of 211 seats held by the Progressive Conservative Party.
The Government felt the need to impose closure to a very minimal opposition consisting of only 40 Liberals and 30 NDP Members. However, I am certain that the voters realize what is going on and that the Opposition will not be this weak for long. The voters will not let a government in whom they have put their confidence shabbily treat the minority in the House of Commons especially in view of the staggering majority won by the party opposite after making all kinds of promises which are quickly being broken one after the other. One of the promises which is being forgotten the most often was to have a continuous process of consultation. Here we now have a perfect example of a Government taking action in an important sector, that of foreign investment, without having consulted anyone.
The only one to speak on behalf of the Progressive Conservative Party this morning, the same Parliamentary Secretary to whom I referred earlier, said that the Government did consult. "Every weekend, we go home to our constituencies, we meet our voters. We receive letters." This is the easy way out.
I am well aware that when Members go back to their constituencies during the weekend, they see a few voters, not necessarily to speak about this matter but rather to solve particular problems and to discuss many other issues where the Progressive Conservative Government is having trouble. For instance, what are the Progressive Conservatives doing to help Quebec pork producers? I am certain that all PC Members who visited their constituencies and met with farmers did not discuss foreign investment and Bill C-15. What they heard was: "When are you going to give us the $13 millions you had promised" This is what the voters were saying last weekend and this is what we can read in the newspapers.
Therefore, there will not be any consultation. Let us put an end to the debate as soon as possible. The only consultation to have taken place is the debate we have been having in this House where Members can rise and say what they think about Bill C-15, an Act respecting foreign investment.
According to the rhetoric of the Progressive Conservative Party, the purpose of Bill C-15 is to attract foreign investment while protecting our national identity. I would like to spend a few minutes speaking about this aspect of the bill. In this regard, the Progressive Conservative Party is trying to step into the shoes of the Liberal Party. During the last few years, which party has attempted, while allowing foreign investment, to provide some protection to several sectors of the Canadian industry if not the Liberal Party? It was a Liberal policy which led to the creation of the Foreign Investment Review Agency better known as FIRA. And whatever the opinion of my NDP colleague who took the floor just before me, he may try to make us believe that it was the New Democratic Party that forced the Liberals to introduce legislation to establish FIRA, but anybody who has followed Canadian politics knows
that the idea sprang from a Liberal convention held in Toronto inl972 when people in attendance, members of the Liberal Party of Canada, recommended to the then federal Liberal Government to create an agency so as to make sure that foreign investments would really benefit the Canadian economy and not jeopardize certain sectors of our economy.
Who decided to impose restrictions on foreign investments in specific sectors such as culture and finance, if not the Liberal Government, the previous administration of the country?
Who decided to approach the European Economic Community in an attempt to diversify the source of foreign investments, if not the Right Hon. Pierre Elliott Trudeau himself when he was Canada's Prime Minister, because one of the great dangers we are facing is to have foreign investments coming mostly from a single source? That is how we can fall directly under legislation adopted by our neighbours to the south and likely to disrupt our economy.
Those protective measures against foreign investments have been implemented by the Liberals and I object to the fact that Progressive Conservative Party representatives now try to argue that the Progressive Conservative Government wants to attract foreign investors, while at the same time safeguarding our national identity. Their defensive approach with respect to our national identity is sheer nonsense, that is not what they are trying to do.
The major argument of the Progressive Conservatives with respect to job creation is now, and was during the election campaign: Let us allow capital to create jobs. That argument has continued to be translated into specific measures. Since business has resumed in the House of Commons, we have heard the Progressive Conservative Government endlessly repeating that we have to let private capital create jobs, and we have also seen that same Government shirk its major responsibility, and that is to create jobs.
We have seen this Government cancel job creation programs, although it keeps saying that creating jobs is its priority. A good example is the elimination of the Summer Canada Program: $75 million that was supposed to create jobs for young Canadians next summer. They have been saying: Let capital create jobs. The new 1985 rhetoric, however, is: Let foreign capital create jobs. An interesting but dangerous shift in Conservative rhetoric. The Government has abdicated its job creating function. It has said: Let Canadian capital create jobs. Now it is saying: Let foreign investment create jobs. This is one way for the Party in power to sympathize with people who are looking for jobs and give the impression that the Government is concerned about creating jobs. However, they are really showing they want to leave it up to foreign capital to create jobs in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, you know as well as I do that the danger here is that foreign companies setting up branches in Canada do so in their own interest. When they come to Canada to buy an
January 28, 1985

existing company, this does not create new employment. What it does create is a situation in which existing jobs, under the new company, are controlled from outside Canada.
When times are hard and the company's market starts to shrink, what is it going to do? Is it going to shut down its Canadian branch and with it the jobs they are promising us today when they say: "Let foreign capital create jobs"? These are temporary jobs, Mr. Speaker. These jobs are liable to vanish into thin air, depending on the international economic situation and international markets.
The Progressive Conservative Party would do well to allow more time for debate in the House on Bill C-15, an Act respecting investment in Canada. We agree to letting foreign capital come into this country. However, as the Liberal Party of Canada, we want substantial guarantees that any foreign investment will be in the interests of Canadians, that it will create long-term and not temporary employment and that the most sensitive sectors of our economy will not be adversely affected.
That is what we are trying to do, Mr. Speaker, while we are considering Bill C-15. We are not trying to prolong debate unnecessarily, but we are trying to obtain a fair deal for Canadians who want to invest and for Canadians who are looking for jobs and are unable to find any.

Mr. Speaker, it is striking, so quickly after the House has returned from the Christmas recess, that the Government is anxious to close debate on this extremely crucial subject. One would think that the debate had been dragging on for weeks. In fact, the Minister brought the Bill before the House before Christmas and there was a limited period of time in which to debate it. It seems a long time since the Bill was introduced, but that is because the Christmas recess was so long. Since the House reconvened a week ago, there have been two Opposition days and there has not been a great focus on the subject matter of the Bill.
I think the reason the closure motion has been brought before the House is that there was a certain amount of momentum, criticism and thrust to the debate which we in this Party and members of the Liberal Party managed to gain in the period before Christmas. The Government, frankly, is fearful that it will again be possible for us to build up this momentum and to develop a sense of critical analysis of this faulty piece of legislation before us.
I have a sense, and I believe perhaps the Government has as well-which is why it has moved this closure motion so quickly-that throughout this country there is now a growing sense of awareness that something is happening here in Ottawa which is dangerous to the future of the country and to our sense of independence. This is an unfortunate effort to ram something through the House which has not been subject to
Investment Canada Act
the kind of scrutiny and careful attention which something of such major importance should receive. We are after all, Mr. Speaker, dealing with something which has been at the heart of economic development concerns in Canada for well over 100 years.
I mentioned in past debate that it was in the 1870s that the first subsidiaries came to Canada. Since that period we have seen a careful and gradual development of public policy with respect to branch plants. Back in the 1870s and 1880s we believed, as this Government seems now to believe, that foreign investment of any kind would be good for the country. But, Mr. Speaker, we have come a long way since 1880. We have learned a great deal since those days. We have seen the problems which can develop in an economy when there is no sense of strategy vis-a-vis foreign investment. That is why we on this side of the House have been so concerned about the abdication of strategy and the absence of policy direction which this new Bill represents.
It is not just those of us who are critical of foreign investment who recognize the problem. Let me indicate to Hon. Members on the government side some of the recognition which is there from those who actually run foreign firms here in this country. For instance, the President of the Sarnia based Dow Chemical of Canada Limited, spoke to the press about drawing some Canadian capital, some Canadian shareholders, into his subsidiary. He said he was concerned about this because "we are the Canadian subsidiary of a multinational. We do not necessarily always operate to do the best we can for our local books. We are attempting to optimize the parent company's books".
What that means, Mr. Speaker, is that the concern with profitability and investment which can benefit this country is not at the heart of the business operations of that subsidiary. Instead, its first priority is to benefit the parent company. I quote the words of David Clark, the President of Campbell Soup Company Ltd., another major subsidiary which operates in southwestern Ontario. He said: "There is the danger of falling into the funny money syndrome of corporate management", the possibility of shifting money out of the country through transactions with the parent company.
For that reason, he and his company welcomed the possibility of having Canadian shareholders in his firm. That brings, as he puts it, "a heightened sense of Financial responsibility. It brings you one step closer to reality". That is the kind of flimflam, the kind of internal corporate shifting of resources, which can take place if we have an economy which is dominated by foreign investment. That is why we need a sense of strategy, a sense of direction and the capacity to review and control the extremely large sector of our country which is controlled by foreign firms.
It is a source of particular concern to me, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister is moving, through his Parliamentary Secretary, for closure of this debate before he has presented to the House hiw own sense of direction with respect to a key part of Bill C-15, that is the part of the Bill which outlines a concern with key cultural parts of our economy.

January 28, 1985
Investment Canada Act
The Minister indicated in his press conference when he introduced this Bill that he would clarify the kinds of sectors with which he expected that part of the Bill to deal and the mechanisms he would use to give the Bill that sense of specific impact. He has not come before the House to provide that sense of direction despite the fact that the Association of Canadian Publishers has gone before the Minister and told him that we need this sense of direction, not just because of a general concern but because of the very specific problem of the takeover of Prentice-Hall in the United States by Gulf and Western. Prentice-Hall is an extremely large American company with a great deal of investment in our cultural sector.
We believe, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister should present us with some sense of how he intends to proceed on this part of his Bill before the Bill receives approval to go to committee. The Association of Canadian Publishers has been very detailed in its comments on Prentice-Hall. It has indicated that there are Canadian buyers who are willing and able to make a purchase of the Canadian subsidiary of Prentice-Hall but the Minister has not provided direction as to how this is going to be possible under the new Bill.
For this reason, Mr. Speaker, this motion is a premature move which we will oppose. We hope the Government will reconsider and withdraw this closure motion at this stage and allow full debate on this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I know Hon. Members of this House would not want to see this Tory closure motion imposed on the House today. It is obvious why the Government is moving closure today. It is because it knows that there is a very great unease in this country about the way in which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is handling the whole question of foreign ownership. He hies himself off to New York and essentially says to the economic community in New York: "Come and take whatever you want. It is up there. There are just no questions asked". There is a great deal of unease about that.
Clearly the Canadian people are concerned about jobs and they want to see Canadian industries prosper and move forward just as much as foreign companies. I believe that is why this Bill should be thoroughly discussed here today. I asked the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) last week how many applications had actually been received under FIRA since the Prime Minister went down to New York and told them to come and buy out whatever they want in Canada, no questions asked. He went into a great deal of flimflam and breast beating and all the rest of it, but he never did indicate the number of applications there have been since this Bill was introduced into the House and since the Cabinet said, to all intents and purposes, "You just have to apply to take over any Canadian company; there will be no questions asked". So I think there is a great deal of unease in the country regarding the Government's intentions.
We believe, Mr. Speaker, that businessmen from western Europe, Japan and the U.S. will invest in Canada when there
is an opportunity. We believe we should welcome that investment provided it is beneficial to our country in terms of job creation, research and development and export development. There is no problem with that. That is why we think the existing rules and regulations of FIRA are desirable.
Some 97 per cent of foreign investment has been approved in the last couple of years, but that does not indicate how many companies were encouraged to do their R and D here or to dedicate a portion of their Canadian production capacity to the international market. Look at the tremendous spurt there has been to the Ontario economy this year. It has grown at a rate of 5 per cent, slightly higher than the national average. In fact, it pushed the national average up by perhaps 1 per cent. Most of that was due to the production of two vehicles, a Chevrolet automobile and a Chrysler mini-van. Some $8 billion worth of autos were produced last year and we will produce some $13 billion worth this year. That has been a tremendous spurt to automobile manufacturing, so to then give away our ability to negotiate with American or other foreign companies just does not seem very wise.
The other thing Tories are very concerned about in having this Bill debated for any length of time is that the Canadian people generally are going to become more familiar with the amount of progress we have made in Canadian ownership. The figures indicate that in mining and smelting Canadian ownership has risen from some 30 per cent in 1970 to something like 52 per cent in 1980. Pretty impressive figures. In 1975 research and development in this country amounted to something like $1 billion. In 1984 it was $5.3 billion. A lot of this is due to the fact we were able to negotiate with foreign investors the amount of research and development they would do.
The Tories are also concerned with the results of our effort to increase Canadian ownership in the oil and gas industry. During the first three years of the National Energy Program Canadian ownership in that industry has risen from 28 per cent to 40 per cent. Oil exploration has increased by 53 per cent from 1980 to 1984. Reserves of natural gas have risen to a record high of some 33 years' supply. The Department of Energy, Mines and Resources projects that we will be self-sufficient in oil on a net basis right through to the end of the century. When the NEP was proposed to Parliament we had dared hope that we would be self-sufficient by 1990. Here we are only three years later and we are up to self-sufficiency on a net basis to the year 2000. So naturally the Tories want to bring in a motion to cut off debate because they are very concerned about people becoming knowledgeable about the Prime Minister's attitude towards foreign investment.
It is also very interesting to see how the Government co-ordinates its policies with those of the Ontario Government. The Premier of Ontario, who has just retired, brought in a 20 per cent land transfer tax many years ago which applied to the sale of land to non-residents. Of course, that completely destroyed part of the business of northern Ontario realtors who were selling cottage lots. Now that we have a Tory Government in Ottawa it will be interesting to see whether there will
January 28, 1985

be negotiations with the provincial government to encourage that kind of investment in the country.
It is also interesting to note a headline in the Toronto Star of January 19 which indicated that the Nissan Corporation of Japan was not planning to make any further investment in Canada in spite of what the Prime Minister is doing with this Investment Canada legislation. He said these companies would be crawling all over themselves to invest in Canada. If we compare the lack of success of the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) this fall with the Nissan Corporation, which incidentally is going to be investing in Great Britain, China, South East Asia and other countries, with the success of Mr. Lumley, the former Minister, last spring, then we see he is not being very successful. Over the course of a three or four month period Mr. Lumley was able to announce a $100 million Honda plant in Ontario resulting in some 350 jobs. He negotiated a new AMC/Renault plant, some $700 million and 7,000 jobs. There were two other GM plants involving 1,100 jobs and a capital investment of over $1.25 billion. If we compare the two, we see Mr. Lumley comes out looking very well because he got $2.1 billion of investment and 10,000 jobs. Obviously the present Government's policies are not working, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, an awful lot of people in the country must be sharing my disappointment. During the election campaign the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his Party indicated that once accorded the robes of power they would look to a new Canadian agenda. The smiling, confidence-building visage from which such promising words issued must have filled the hearts of many Canadians with the idea that they would share in determining the destiny of this country in accord with the high-sounding phrases heard during the election. We heard then and have heard since that the process of government would change from one of confrontation to one of consultation. In particular it was said that the Opposition would be consulted on all matters to ensure that the House acted in the interests of the people of the country.
We expected that these pronouncements would reflect new year's resolutions for 1985. As one of the first acts of the Government we are faced with a motion to close debate on something of such fundamental importance to the Canadian people as this legislation called Investment Canada. It must be a rather strange spectacle to almost all people of the world to see a Canadian Prime Minister going to New York to announce that Canada's destiny will be built there.
Only a few days ago I spoke in London, Ontario and there encountered immigrants from Argentina and Chile. They said to me that it is too bad that the Canadian people are not as aware as they should be of the debate going on in the House of Commons these days. I wish it were possible for the Canadian people to understand the implications of the legislation before the House in terms of the experience of the people of South America. If we want to have control over our Government,
Investment Canada Act
economy and future, we must be careful to learn the lessons of South and Central America well. We know what kind of contribution unencumbered American investment and input will have on those three facets of our existence.
If it were not so serious, it would almost be laughable to recount the purposes outlined for Investment Canada. In the background is the assumption that Canadians, by wanting to control their own economy, are somehow a little perverted, that we are and have been discouraging investment through FIRA, and that if we eliminate FIRA the whole world is going to come in with truck loads of dollars to help us out. In fact there is every evidence in the world that foreign investment, and particularly American investment, has not been materially affected during the course of FIRA given the competition that we face from other potential sources for great profits for American investors.
No matter what analysis one may apply to the evidence for that statement, there is no indication that the adoption of Investment Canada is going to mean the great surge of investment from the United States that the Government would have us hope for. Even if it does occur, we are told quite clearly by the Americans that the only lucrative area for investment for them is in our primary resources. You can bet that that will not be on the basis of generating jobs for Canadians in Canada. Such investment will not be based on Canadian priorities.
Let us review this piece of legislation which the Government does not want to have debated in too much detail because the Canadian people may find out too much about it and the repercussions it has for Canada. If this motion were defeated and the debate allowed to continue, a level of duplicity that would astound Canadians would be revealed in terms of what this Bill says it is going to do and what it actually proposes to do.
It proposes to create more jobs but one can look at every detail and word in legislation and find not a single provision which would ensure new Canadian jobs. It proposes that it will increase exports for Canada. However, there is not a line or word in this legislation which would provide for increased exports. The Bill suggests that there will be increased research and development in Canada. One can study every line and detail an find no provision for increased research and development in Canada.
The Government says that by virtue of this legislation there will be increased technological diffusion. That is nonsensical, as indicated by the fact that no attempt has been made to provide for it in the legislation. A sorry piece of nonsense has been presented to the Canadian people and the House. I can understand that the Government wants to close debate as quickly as possible before the Canadian people discover what it is all about.
We do not want Canada to be sold to others. If one goes anywhere in Canada where there is forestry, mining, fishing or agriculture and asks the ordinary people who are not going to be blessed with the huge profits which come from productivity and innovation how they feel about selling Canada's future
