subtopic: ELECTION OF MR. FRANK MILLER AS ONTARIO PREMIER DESIGNATE
ELECTION OF MR. FRANK MILLER AS ONTARIO PREMIER DESIGNATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Ontario's longstanding tradition of selecting superb Premiers has continued, in spades. It gives me the utmost pleasure to tell the House that Frank Miller, my provincial counterpart from Muskoka, is the province's new Premier designate.
I believe that the choice made by delegates on Saturday night shows insight and political savvy. Despite the strong opposition mounted by other candidates, Mr. Miller won the confidence of the Party.
He has gained a reputation for fairness and hard work as a Cabinet Minister in Ontario, with four different portfolios.
ISJr. Miller was offered widespread support from the people who know him best, the folks from Parry Sound-Muskoka. He secured the confidence of all sectors of society throughout his political career.
With these congratulations to Frank Miller today, I must also express the Province of Ontario's indebtedness to Premier Bill Davis. The people of Ontario are indeed fortunate to have men such as these aspire to hold the position of Premier.
I declare without hesitation that I am most anxious to be a part of Miller's Ontario in the years to come. We have been ably led in Ontario's past, and now we may look forward to a bright and shining future. It's Miller time.

subtopic: DESTRUCTION BY FIRE OF FISH PLANT AT GLACE BAY, N.S.
DESTRUCTION BY FIRE OF FISH PLANT AT GLACE BAY, N.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the news this morning carried a story of yet another major economic blow being struck against Glace Bay in Cape Breton. A fire has destroyed a fish processing plant which was the last major employer in a community already suffering more than 50 per cent unemployment. Only last year the fire in No. 26 Colliery threw 1,200 people out of work.
While Glace Bay is a tragic example, it is only one example of the kind of unemployment facing people throughout Cape Breton. Unfortunately the new Conservative Government has reacted by cutting programs which would have reduced this unemployment. One of the first Conservative measures was to
January 28, 1985

eliminate the transfer of its Income Security Branch from Halifax to Sydney.
The federal Government must involve itself in a program to deal with the tragic unemployment in Cape Breton. Sydney Steel's business plan must be implemented in consultation with the workers in order to guarantee that economic benefits are passed on to the people of that hard hit area. The situation is now critical, and we desperately require some tangible solutions.

Mr. Speaker, with the exception of the Senate there is probably no other part or agency of Government that has been subjected to so many studies ad infinitum as has the Northern Canada Power Commission.
The previous Liberal Government always set up yet more studies instead of addressing the many real and outstanding problems. Northerners expect the new Government to take positive action. The principal recommendations of the Penner Report on NCPC should be implemented forthwith.
Jurisdiction over power supply in the Territories should be devolved from the federal to the territorial Governments. The territorial public utility boards should become the regulatory agencies rather than the National Energy Board favoured by the previous administration. Provision must be made for tying in the southern Territories to the existing Alberta power grid. The questions of rate rationalization and subsidization in remote diesel supplied areas must be properly resolved.
Yes, it is expected of the new Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) that he take action and not just avoid and set aside the problems as did his predecessor.

subtopic: IMPORTANCE OF CADET SUMMER CAMP PROGRAM
IMPORTANCE OF CADET SUMMER CAMP PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Monday the Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne) made some lofty pronouncements in connection with the beginning of International Youth Year. While 1985 will be important in terms of highlighting youth concerns, what young people in Canada want more than anything else is work and not words.
Some 80,000 young people who had jobs last summer under the Summer Canada Program have been left dangling while the Government fiddles, frets, and fools with the program that was working perfectly well.
One part of the Summer Canada Program that has been left high and dry by the cuts made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is the Cadet Summer Camp Program which was cut by nearly $1 million.
Working with Summer Canada funding, the Navy, Army and Air Cadets, in conjunction with the Department of National Defence, put together an extremely valuable and worthwhile endeavour for our youth. Cadet summer camps gave young people a better understanding of what it means to be a Canadian. It helped them develop their qualities of self reliance and leadership, and gave them the opportunity to meet other young Canadians from other parts of Canada. Cutting $85 million from Summer Canada without announcing a substitute program was un unusual, cruel, and insensitive move even for this Government.
I call on the Government to ensure that whatever new program is announced, the Cadet Summer Program will not be affected.

Mr. Speaker, significant numbers of Canadians attend courses at accredited universities in the United States. To accommodate working adults who cannot afford the luxury of taking off work for extended periods of time, some universities condense an entire semester of studies into a few short but very intensive weeks.
One of my constituents was able to complete the equivalent of one full semester in seven weeks of summer study at an American university. The tuition was some $2,000.
My constituent, Mr. Snell, was surprised to learn that these tuition fees were not income tax deductible because the classes attended in the United States were not of at least 13 weeks' duration.
In searching for the rationale behind such a restriction, one can only assume concerns on the part of Government that the taxpayers of Canada might be partially financing summer vacations outside the country. Such an assumption does a disservice to those Canadians who would wish to pursue their education legitimately and who, plainly and simply, cannot afford to leave their employment for 13 or more weeks.
I suggest changes to Section 60, the tuition fee deductibility provisions of the Income Tax Act to accommodate those Canadians attending legitimate credit courses of any duration at accredited educational institutions, whether these institutions be inside Canada our outside Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it is my understanding that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) will be meeting with his ministerial advisory committee tomorrow in Vancouver to discuss a West Coast salmon vessel buy-back program.
It is my understanding that this will be involving the federal Government in a $100 million buy-back program for West Coast salmon fishing vessels. The federal Government expects to recover $40 million through the sale of these vessels. In addition, the federal Government intends to extract $200 million from West Coast salmon fishermen over the next 10 years by imposing a landing tax which could be as high as 13.5 per cent of the landed value of the catch.
Further, it is my understanding that in the final analysis the buy-back of vessels will be paid for by Pacific Coast salmon fishermen. Over all the federal Government, through the landing tax on fishing vessels, will earn a profit of $150 million from the program over 10 years. The real beneficiaries of this program will be the banks which are being bailed out. Fishermen will pay over $200 million in landing tax costs, and many thousands of British Columbians will lose their jobs as a result of the Government's buy-back program.
It would be useful if the Minister would confirm that he is meeting with his ministerial advisory committee this week, that he is discussing the proposals for the buy-back, and that he would, unlike the fishing treaty, provide Hon. Members of the House and of the standing committee with the documents related to the proposals for a buy-back program.

Mr. Speaker, as spokesman for 6,000 or more people who are directly employed by the petrochemical industries in Sarnia-Lambton, and the
12,000	who indirectly owe their livelihood to the chemical valley, I should like to say that there is a positive attitude toward the Government's attention to the hydrocarbon energy sector.
However, there exists a disparity which requires our immediate action. Our major oil-based petrochemical companies, in direct competition with the American Gulf Coast concerns, have been hit hard by the recent drop in the price of west Texas crude oil, a feedstock which compares with our Canadian light crude. This drop in the American price has altered the framework of petrochemical pricing. This has our Canadian companies operating at a distinct disadvantage. While dialogue is ongoing between the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney), the provinces, and the
private sector, on establishing a new oil energy policy, something toward an interim arrangement for the oil dependent petrochemical industry is imperative.

Mr. Speaker, last December the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Greni-er) told the people of Canada, particularly people in the area of Hamilton, that she would be reinstating the Herring Gull program in view of the environmental cuts which had been made. I indicated in the House last Tuesday that the program had in fact not been reinstated and that of the original six, including two biologists and a chemist who were working on the program, only one had been reinstated with instructions simply to collect the eggs, not to do any analysis of the gull deformities which were beginning to show up in terms of the testing.
In telling Canadians that she reinstated the program following pressure from this side of the House, as well as from environmentalists across Canada, the Minister has misled them. Not only has she misled Canadians, but when I raised the issue with her almost a week ago in the House of Commons, I received from her office a form letter which was sent out to Canadians inquiring about the seagull program that dealt with the issue of seagulls and their problems with airplanes.
The Minister has shown the people of Canada, as well as the House of Commons, that she is prepared to distort the truth in her own political interests. The only solution, in view not only of her refusal to reinstate the program in full but her misleading of Canadian people, is for the Minister to resign.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as a courtesy to my colleagues, with respect to the business for tomorrow it is my intention to have the House consider the same business we are considering today. It is our intention to do the same thing.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Stevens that Bill C-15, an Act respecting investment in Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Regional Development; and on the motion of Mrs. Tardif (Charlesbourg) (p. 1708).

Mr. Speaker, I find it regrettable that we should start this week in Parliament with a motion of closure for a debate as important as Bill C-15, legislation that may affect the very existence of a number of small Canadian businesses.
Mr. Speaker, opinion polls have indicated that 70 per cent of Canadians believe that our economic potential is severely threatened by this kind of foreign control.
After a consensus was reached on the need for ensuring that foreign investment would have a positive impact on the Canadian economy, the Liberal Government at the time created FIRA in the early seventies. As the Gray Report mentioned in 1972, when considering foreign investment one should bear in mind three potential dangers. First, distortion of
January 28, 1985

the international market as a result of other governments intervening to serve their own interests. Second, the fact that multinational corporations are liable to ignore local interests and decide on the location of functions such as research and development and advanced processing without considering national economic objectives. Third, Mr. Speaker, the existence of a few international corporations that largely dominate certain sectors and do not react to market forces in the same way as much smaller businesses.
Investment Canada will have only 75 days to approve investment requests submitted for analysis. After 75 days approval is automatic. The Canadian Government is either being incredibly naive or has some perverse desire to sabotage its own program. Anyone who is remotly familiar with the ramifications of multinationals knows that it is impossible to finalize, with in so short a time, the kind of analysis required to approve an investment project. This Government wants to make Investment Canada a paper tiger with no efficiency whatsoever.
Another point is that where up to now, persons applying for foreign investment had to prove that the investment would be of significant benefit to Canada, from now on they merely have to prove that the investment will result in a net benefit. The Canadian Government is putting the financial wellbeing of thousands of small Canadian businesses in jeopardy. This policy of the Progressive Conservatives will considerably diminish the Government's ability to ensure that foreign investment is of benefit not only to the investors but also to the Canadian economy. Foreign investors tend to invest mainly in the small- and medium-sized business sector. In 1980, 40 per cent of investments went to the manufacturing sector, 12.7 per cent to the financial sector and 7.6 per cent to the retail industry. Investors are of course mainly interested in the most profitable sectors and those that rely on advanced technology. Does "Canada is open for business" mean to the Progressive Conservative Party that-

Our industries have to close their door to any hope of development?

Does that slogan mean: For the sake of a few tax dollars, let us stamp out the future of our small businesses, let us destroy the growth potential of our international markets, and let us set up a colonial system?
An area like that of high technology, generally consisting of small companies, could soon wind up in foreign hands. With the multinational corporations' policy of restricted mandates, our industries would be totally paralyzed with respect to advanced technology development. What would prevent a foreign corporation first from taking over a Canadian competitor, then from striking off its research and development budget, and restricting its export potential to promote the sale of the parent company's products on the international market?
Investment Canada Act
The Progressive Conservative Government knows very well, Mr. Speaker, that the policy of restricted mandates is widespread and always kept secret by the corporation. Small and medium-sized businesses are the spearheads of our Canadian economy. They have generated 70 percent of all new private sector jobs during the last decade. The Progressive Conservative Government, which has always boasted about being the advocate of free enterprise, will in fact surrender our small businesses to investors whose prime interest often will be to prevent them from competing with the parent company's products.
Mr. Speaker, this House should take the time needed to debate this foreign investment issue, because the future of our small businesses, which are responsible for creating most jobs, could be endangered. They could fall into the hands of foreign investors.

Mr. Speaker, I thank you for recognizing me. I am sorry you were not in the chair when I was wearing my kilt on Robbie Burns day. I know you would have had some brief comment on that. Perhaps it is better that you were not in the chair, now that I think about it.
I would like to speak on this motion. I have spoken on the previous amendment to this Bill and I would draw Your Honour's attention to the speech I made at that time. I would like to add a few things today. I understand that we are debating a motion of closure. Isn't it amazing, Mr. Speaker, how soon this Conservative Government has fallen into the pattern of the previous Liberal Government? This is an important matter which deals with the future of Canada, investment in Canada, the economic policy of Canada, and maybe even the independence of Canada. Yet we find that the Government wants to close off debate on this issue very quickly.
I can remember the days when the Conservatives on this side of the House stood up, one after the other, and spoke against closure. Right away we have a closure motion. There is an expression, "Plus qa change, plus c'est pared". It means the more things change the more they stay the same. The same words were used in a letter by one of the Conservative Members complaining to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) about the Conservatives being in the lap of the oil industry and not having much of a policy for the consumer. He used those same words, as I do in this particular debate.
In my previous speech on this matter I pointed out that we should not be afraid of FIRA. All FIRA did was to apply a number of tests. Did this foreign investment mean that there were going to be Canadian jobs? Did it mean that the company was going to invest and buy in Canada? Did it mean that the company was going to do its research in Canada? Did it mean that there would be adequate opportunities for jobs for Canadians? It was in fact very practical legislation. If I do have any criticism of FIRA, it would be that it could have

January 28, 1985
Investment Canada Act
been administered better. The proceedings could have taken place more quickly for the businesses involved. However, you do not throw the baby out with the bath water; you reform F1RA. Instead we have Investment Canada.
In the very effective speech of the Member who spoke just before me, he said that Canada was open for business now under this new test. What does that mean? When Canada was open for business in the past our oil industry was suddenly taken over and controlled by foreigners. These foreign-con-trolled companies tended to do their research and development in their home country, mainly the United States. The dividends went out of our country and back to the parent country. Materials were bought from parent companies in another country. Canadians lost in research and development, in money flowing out of the country, and in jobs. We created a branch plant economy.
I grew up in Etobicoke, which I do not admit very often since I represent a riding in Vancouver. However, the truth is that I grew up in Etobicoke. I remember that the branch plant economy brought us prosperity for a number of years. However, there were problems with that kind of economy and when the recession came we began to suffer more than the United States. In times of financial difficulty the branch plants' production would simply go back to their head offices and the head offices would do all of the business rather than the branch plants.
I see a Member from Toronto on the other side who is one of the more attentive Members of the House. I know that he would be interested in this. The key debate in this country, other than on universality which is going on behind the scenes, will be on free trade in the future. The worst of all possible worlds that we could have in Canada is to have free trade with a branch plant economy. We could be in real trouble as an independent country.
That is why I object to this Investment Canada Bill. I believe it indicates that we have given up the attempt to have an independent Canadian industry. The New Democratic Party will not give that up in Canada. In the last few years the oil industry has moved from being 28 per cent Canadian controlled to being 40 per cent Canadian controlled. That is the type of thing we like to see. It does not have to be all public. It can be a mixture of public and private. That is the way we are doing things in Canada these days. We should not give up that thrust because it is the key to an independent country.
I would like to discuss an issue about which people probably do not know much. It has to do with the oil industry. Chevron or Standard Oil of California took over Gulf in the United States. There are companies in Canada called Gulf Canada and Chevron Canada. In fact, Chevron owns Gulf. Under the old legislation, which I believe still applies, Chevron will have to apply to FIRA, as I believe it has, to deal with the situation in Canada since there has been a takeover in the United States. I predict that we may see a reverse takeover. We may see Gulf taking over Chevron.
This is a very strange situation but it gives us a great opportunity. We should use the opportunity, as should the Government, to encourage Canadian individuals, co-operatives or governments to buy Gulf. In this way we could get much more Canadianization. However, the trend is all the other way. This is an opportunity to get Canadian entrepreneurs or the public sector to take over Gulf because of what has happened as a result of takeovers in the United States. Takeovers in the United States affect Canada. Remember that Gulf is involved in Hibernia on the East Coast, in the Beaufort Sea in the north, and vast land tracts and service stations throughout Canada. These issues have not been debated in Canada but should be.
When FIRA was set up its purpose was not to say no to foreign capital but to screen it and make it work for Canadians. Every country does that. It is not as though Canada is the odd person out. They have FIRA in the United States but they call it the American Congress. Takeovers in the United States are investigated by the American Congress, as are changes in taxation laws and so on. Right now in the American Congress a congressional committee is investigating the fact that Canadians own over 6 per cent of the natural gas industry. The Americans are concerned about that for the same reasons that we were concerned when we set up FIRA. They want to ensure that American interests are protected. When Norway or Germany consider these matters it is to ensure that their own interests are protected.
We have an open world. I am a westerner now and I have the religion. I believe in open trade. We need open trade and investment. We are going to get a lot of investment from South East Asia. It is already coming into my province of British Columbia. We must ensure that that investment is used for jobs for Canadians. It must not just come in, take over things and repatriate profits. It must not be allowed to do all its research and development and buying elsewhere. That will not develop our country or reduce our persistently high level of unemployment.
I am a Scot who came over to Canada at the age of five. That is the same age Sir John A. Macdonald was when he came over. I have always been a great fan of Sir John A. Macdonald. I think Sir John A. Macdonald would not think very much of this legislation. The more traditional Conservative policy was to try to develop an independent Canada in which we would rely on each other, our home investment and home markets, as much as possible. While it over-simplifies the situation somewhat, it would have been Sir John A. Macdonald's position.
Bill C-15 is a departure from the traditional Conservative policy. I have real fears that the passage of this Bill will jeopardize the future independence of our country. We will be a branch plant economy controlled by outsiders and we will have even less control over our economy than we have now.

Mr. Speaker, let me say that 1 consider this policy issue contained in Bill C-15
January 28, 1985

to be much too important to have closure imposed upon it so soon. The debate surrounding Bill C-15 is not whether there should or should not be a review process or whether there should be a means or method of reviewing foreign investment. The question is, will the remaining process after Bill C-15 goes into effect continue to be effective and be at all adequate in serving the national interest?
In introducing this Bill, the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) said that we will retain a review process and a review of foreign investment. Strangely enough, he went on to say that by exempting new business and limiting review to larger acquisitions only, we will reduce by 90 per cent the number of transactions now subject to review. The Minister then argues that we must have a review mechanism and proceeds significantly to reduce even the little effectiveness which FIRA had.
In 1973 when the FIRA legislation was being debated in the House, I described it as being a cautious Bill. I looked back to those debates and I noticed that the Hon. Member for York-Simcoe at that time, the present Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion, followed me in debate and agreed with me that it was indeed cautious. Everyone knows that FIRA rarely blocked any investment. In fact, between 1974 when the Bill came into effect and 1984, 92 per cent of all cases which needed a decision were allowed. We can conclude very quickly that foreign investors had nothing to fear from FIRA.
Why, then, did foreign investors object to FIRA? Why did they put pressure on the Conservative Party to do away with FIRA if they formed the Government? I think it is very simple. Foreign investors can sometimes be even more secretive than governments. A review process helps us know what foreign investors are doing and what they will do with the money they bring into Canada. Now, 90 per cent of all of the screening of FIRA will be eliminated by Bill C-15. More often than not, foreign investment means quite simply foreign ownership and control.
When the FIRA legislation was introduced in the late 1970's, Canadians knew that foreign ownership and control had a significant impact in all areas of our life, politically, economically and culturally. Much of that impact is negative.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) recently said that under this legislation Canada is now open for business again. That called for the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) to say, quite correctly, that we have always been open for business. Everyone knows that we have always been open for business. The real question is whether we are now going to be up for sale.
Let me refer Hon. Members to a very important report that was produced by the External Affairs Committee during that same period just prior to the FIRA legislation. It is known as the Wahn report named after Mr. Ian Wahn, who was a Member at that time. That report clearly pointed out a main thesis, that if we get ourselves into a position of economic dependency we lose our freedom to decide on political questions in our interest. That is what worries me so much about
Investment Canada Act
unlimited, uncontrolled and unreviewed foreign investment such as we will have with Bill C-15.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Government House Leader)
speechtext: That is not true.

It is true and I will demonstrate why it is true. When we speak of foreign investment, we talk about foreign ownership and control. That must concern us.
We are not talking about the importation of capital. We are not talking about floating bond issues outside the country. That never was a matter of concern to FIRA and it is not a matter of concern now. We are talking about ownership and control of industries, resources and businesses in Canada. The existence of a foreign investment review business in this country simply means that we can weigh the negative and positive impacts against the national interest. The national interest includes jobs. Will there be jobs? Will there be new technology? Will some of the disadvantaged regions of this country experience more rapid development? I urge Members on the Government side carefully to consider the argument that the review process should not be weakened at this time in our history. This is the time to strengthen it.
Let us consider what is taking place in Australia. The Austrialians welcome foreign investment just as we do. However, they have a policy which seeks to ensure that there is Australian participation and control in industries and resources to an appropriate extent in each particular case. That is the function of their review process.
Bill C-15 goes in the opposite direction. It means, in answer to my hon. friend opposite, that the Canadian interest can be totally disregarded in 90 per cent of all cases. That is what the legislation says. If the Hon. Member can argue contrary to that, I am prepared to sit down and listen to those arguments. This is not a valid, enlightened or acceptable public policy position. Bill C-15 takes a modest, non-threatening review process and replaces it with a carte blanche. In 1977 and 1982 the Liberal Government made some moves to reduce the power of FIRA. Investment ceilings were raised so that there could be a shorter procedure rather than going through the full review process. I would have argued against that had I been in the Government, but the times seemed to dictate that that was the way we should proceed.
It is important to remember that the review process remained intact. I am not concerned about the Government changing the name. It can call it Investment Canada rather than FIRA; that is not relevant. However, there must be a mechanism in place by which we can review foreign investment. It is irresponsible not to have such a mechanism.
The Minister's statement on Bill C-15 is terribly misleading. He said: "We believe that Canada requires a means to safeguard its national interests". He goes on to say that there must be a review process and then, in another statement in the same document, he says that they will exempt new investment and anything except large acquisitions. This means that 90 per cent of foreign investment will not be reviewed at all. It means that the Government is doing away with the review process, so

January 28, 1985
Investment Canada Act
there is a clear contradiction in the Minister's own statement. He cannot have it both ways.
The doors of Canada are being thrown wide open. My concern is that we will not get the benefit that we expect. I do not believe that we will get the jobs and the new technologies that are referred to in the Minister's statement. We will not get the regional economic expansion and development. What will be the Government's next step when it comes to realize that? What further steps will it take to entice the flow of foreign investment into this country for more ownership and control? In the 1970s Canadians were deeply concerned about this question. At that time the Gallup polls indicated that there was concern about foreign economic domination of Canada. They said that the Government had done too little before the FIRA legislation was brought in and that more action was required. FIRA was part of that response, and I want to tell the House that it has worked. The percentage of foreign ownership in Canada has been reduced significantly.
Today the concern about foreign ownership and control is blunted. It is less of a concern to Canadians because their preoccupation, quite rightly so, is with high rates of unemployment. Surely the Government is not saying to Canadians today that Bill C-15 is their answer to the problem of unemployment. If so, they will be sadly disappointed. Bill C-15 will not create jobs. As 90 per cent of all foreign investment will not be reviewed, Canadians will be in the dark about whether the national interest will be served as a result of such investment, or whether there will be benefits to our country. When the dawn breaks we may realize that the price we paid has been too high and our independence may have been reduced to puppetry.
Economic nationalism does not mean being insular or defensive; it means taking positive steps to strengthen Canada's position at home and abroad. A foreign investment review process does that, but Bill C-15 does not. In its wild charge in its effort to shoot down Liberal policies of the past, I am afraid the Government is shooting itself in the foot.

Mr. Speaker, this is a sad day for the Canadian nation. Today the House of Commons debates, under the compulsion of not being able to place any more amendments on the resolution before it, a Bill in which the principles of building up the country so that it will be under our own control, as my colleagues in both caucuses have said, are being sacrificed. Indeed, this is a sad day for the Conservative Party. Over many years that Party, more often than not, has had a sense of national development. As the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) pointed out so well, under its first Leader under Confederation it worked toward national development with a variety of national policies. Much more recently and under the leadership of the late Right Hon. Member for Prince Albert, it attempted to develop policies of national development which gave nothing to the desire of others, whether they be in the United States or in Great Britain, to control the economic
development of this country. Having introduced that heritage in our midst, I wonder how the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) feels as the House of Commons debates these measures.
The sense of a development of our resources and our economy in the interests of Canadians and the sense of a process which will be under the control of Canadian people have been abandoned. Instead we have a Party which is clearly dominated by the principles of neo-classic economics that were powerful in the post-war era, principles which in earlier years its members had the good sense to criticize, if not to reject. Those principles are now triumphant. In the Party which governs this country now, we have a Party of neo-colonialism. As is well understood in many parts of the world, it is a Party which does not think the economy, resources and opportunities of this country can be developed by Canadians in the interests of Canadians. Rather, it is a Party which thinks that this has to be done by others, and that it is all important to obtain, somehow or other, the capital which will make it possible for some people to find employment in the country. Given that conviction, it thinks that the only possibility of greater prosperity is to turn its back on the traditions of the past and throw the door wide open to capitalists from wherever to let them do what they will in this country. That kind of neo-classic economic thinking for many years has been regarded as being powerful in the Liberal Party. Today, incredibly, it is the policy of the Conservative Party of Canada.
Former colleagues of mine in the academic community have devoted a good deal of attention to the question of where these ideas were stronger. Given the inspiration of the late Professor Donald Creighton, those ideas were strong in the Liberal Party, and the Liberal Party sold out the country. The curious point about that notion as it was being developed in the seventies, according to the writings of John Hutcheson, was that the Liberal Party was moving very slowly and tentatively from one study and one report to another study and another report. Eventually it was recognized, albeit with the help of the New Democratic Party during those minority government days from 1972 to 1974, that some sort of control on foreign investment was essential. In those days the Liberal Government established the Foreign Review Investment Agency.
If one wondered whether by their actions they were belying the reputation which others had assigned to them, that it was the Conservative Party which actually deserved to be seen as the Party of international liberalism without any regard for national development being in our own hands, these days it becomes clear, as the Liberals stand with us in defending FIRA, that the Conservative Government, in pursuing its own misguided convictions, is setting out to sell out the country.
As a result, what are the prospects? We have a Government which is desperately convinced in its own mind that it is only the decisions of those with money or with capital to invest which hold out any hope for us. However, as those who have travelled to Wall Street in the last weeks have told us clearly, to change the Canadian law will not be enough. Capitalists
January 28, 1985

will not be interested in us unless they see some really good opportunity from which to profit.
How will that happen? I suppose that one way to make Canada attractive would be to have wage levels which would undercut those of others. However, in a world in which Asian countries in particular are powerful competitors and in which the wage rates of many countries run lower than ours, is that the prospect which the Government holds out, that we drive down wages by one means or another until the country becomes tempting on the wage rate level? What other factors which might produce costs will we have to abandon? Will occupational health and safety go by the boards? Will the labour relations laws be dropped? These are the kinds of questions upon which my colleagues have focused. They have asked about the development of free economic zones in this country. They are immediately relevant. How, in fact, will we get back foreign capital to Canada which is supposed to provide employment? Surely it is by contemplating dire fates of that sort that we find any reason at all to think that it might arrive.
The prospect of investment in order to supply the Canadian market, particularly at the same time as the Government considers reductions in tariffs and freer and freer trade arrangements, seems to be very limited. It is particularly limited when we have a Government which does not have a wise sense of the need to build demand in Canada. It does not deal with the deficit by reducing tax expenditures which we considered last week in the House, tax expenditures which may well amount to more than the amount by which the budget is in deficit. If that were to be the case, it would be obvious that individual Canadian taxpayers would be grossly overtaxed. That would be one good reason, the soundest reason, for knowing that the Canadian market and the Canadian consumers do not have the means to sustain the demand which the country needs.
We can see on these matters of the economic situation in Canada that there is little reason to hope that the establishment of Investment Canada will solve our economic difficulties. We will end up with the same situation we experienced before. Capital may come in. The inevitable accompaniment of that is the increased technology of other people, reduced opportunity for research and development in this country, and less employment for engineers and scientists.
We will see less opportunity for employment of managers. There will be no possibility of rising to the top of these companies within the Canadian context. We will see particular distortions of trade patterns, excessive imports of manufactured goods, and buying from the parent rather than from Canadian manufacturers and other Canadian industries. There will be increased exports of raw materials without their being worked up in Canada. On both counts there will be less employment in this country. There will be capital outflows.
If there is no close consideration of the benefits to flow from foreign investment, why in God's name do we want to have the
Investment Canada Act
stuff? If we are going to let other people profit from it with very little spinoff for us, we face every possibility that the investment could take the form of buying out companies in this country, taking control of them and shutting them down. That could follow directly from the results of this Government's policies.
How can anyone regard what the Conservative Government has put before us in Bill C-15 as being conducive to the economic development of this country? The legislation is a disaster. It is to be profoundly regretted in the national interests that the Government faces us today with the closure of debate on this second reading.

Mr. Speaker, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) told a New York audience that Canada was open for business, some of us were greatly surprised. We wondered what on earth he could mean, because Canada had always been open for business.
The Bill before us contains a lot of puffery and a lot of general stuff. The only significant part seems to be that the name of the foreign investment agency is going to be changed. A large proportion of potential foreign investment in Canada will now be free of the necessity of any review. It is perhaps this that leads one to wonder what indeed is the hidden agenda of the Government, because there is no independent sovereign state that I know of that does not have some limitations or some screening of foreign investment to ensure that it meets national goals.
The much criticized Foreign Investment Review Agency allowed about 90 per cent of the applications. It was receptive to foreign investment in Canada as long as that investment was shown to be in the national interest. The language in the FIRA Bill was "of significant benefit to Canada". The Bill before us will require that the investment be of net benefit to Canada. We have not yet had a clear explanation of the reason for changing those words.
There are many issues of key importance in this legislation and that are worthy of serious discussion at second reading stage. I deplore the Government's decision to introduce closure at this stage. When the Opposition is so small in numbers, surely the Government could have refrained from using its massive majority and allowed these serious matters to be discussed in some depth.
High levels of foreign investment will certainly be crucial to Canada during the next few years. A Conference Board of Canada study highlighted that. It is something we all know. There is no evidence whatever that the Bill before us will attract new investment. With the current massive U.S. trade deficit and the great difficulties which many sectors in the U.S. economy face in modernizing their economy, there is no reason to think that we can expect a large flow of American capital here in the next few years. At best or at worst, depending on your point of view, we may find that some American investors will park their money here in a short-term way while looking for the best long term investment in their home country. This is being made very easy by this legislation

January 28, 1985
Investment Canada Act
which has no requirements, or at least a minimum of them, for the benefit of Canada. Certainly new investment is being excluded from screening, except in certain cases to which I will return.
The Conservative Party has always detested FIRA. However, let me give one example of a case where FIRA would have saved much heartache. A couple of years ago a proud man was in my office in tears. The firm for which he worked had been established in Canada prior to FIRA. It was an American branch plant. It suddenly closed its doors. When he went to work on a Monday, the firm had disappeared. It was a branch plant operation that we saw before FIRA where there was no R and D done in Canada, no attempt to upgrade the skills of employees, and marketing decisions were made in the United States.
When this firm decided it would be in its interests to move to one of the southern States where there are no unions and they could pay minimum wages, all they had to do was to close the doors and move everything out over a weekend. After 20 years, this man, with no marketable skills, found himself unemployed.
That kind of human tragedy was being repeated all across Ontario. It is the kind of thing that FIRA was meant to avoid. With FIRA there was a requirement and an insistence that the investor provide some research and development in Canada and create a situation where, if the firm left, the workers would have some skills and assets.
Another concern about this proposed Bill, which will take off most requirements for review, is the degree of autonomy in decision-making within subsidiaries. This question of absentee decision-making has been raised often in this House. I have given one example of it. There are many cases where decisions being made about the Canadian workplace by people outside Canada is fraught with potential difficulties.
FIRA approved 90 per cent of the applications before it. However, what went on before the approval was a negotiation process aimed at getting the best deal for Canada. The bottom line in this is still, where is the pay-off for Canadians? Is it consistent with Canada's long-term interests to open the door wide to investment without any requirement that that investment be in Canadian interests? The Bill does allow for review in certain cases, but these cases have not been sufficiently clarified in this very brief second reading debate. In my view, they should be clarified even before the matter goes to committee.
The Bill does allow for review when the investment affects Canada's cultural heritage and national identity, but that statement makes a very broad sweep. What issues does the Government propose to include in this and what control by regulation will exist? Will it include oil, gas, mining, and uranium? How often and in which situations will the Government use its reserved power?
What about the review process? As the Bill is written, it looks as though all power rests in the Minister's hands. Is this
desirable? Should there not be other methods of review? These are questions to which our Party will be looking for very clear answers in committee and in the House when the Bill returns at report stage.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is the House ready for the question? Debate.

Mr. Speaker, we are not quite ready for the question yet. It may well be that at some point we will be ready for the question but we will certainly let you know when that is so, Sir.
I just finished having a conversation with certain people in the lobby. I had a chat with one of the pages, in fact, and I said to her: "You have listened to this debate at some length. Is there anything you think I might raise on your behalf as you are one of the young people affected by the inadequate policies of the previous Government and equally or even more detrimentally affected by the inadequate policies of this Government?"
I found her response to be very interesting. She said that this was an important debate and that young people recognized the importance of this debate but that what they really wanted to know was where they were going to find summer jobs this year. They wanted to know where they were going to find employment for this coming summer that would enable them to continue at school as we would wish them to do. I thought that the relevance of that comment was clear. She was really saying, "Why are we doing this right now? Why are we not dealing with what is no doubt the major issue before the country? Why are we not dealing with the question of where the people who are now unemployed might find employment at this point in time?"
It makes absolutely no difference to the current status of the 1.5 million people who are now unemployed whether the Government does or does not have this legislation passed in this current session. I took from the comment of the page that while she could see the value of the debate on foreign investment and, in fact, encouraged further discussion and a more careful analysis of it, she was asking me if it were not possible to move on and deal with matters of immediate relevance. Do you know something, Mr. Speaker? There is a lot to be said for that point of view.
I believe you, Mr. Speaker, and most Members here have travelled in their constituencies recently and have found as I did that the single question that is uppermost in the minds of the overwhelming majority of the people with whom I spoke, and I suspect with whom other Members spoke as well, was the state of the unemployed. They wanted to know whether they would Find jobs. If I understand the economic processes and the social programs of this country correctly, and I think I do, this legislation, important though the Minister in charge of it may think it is and relevant though the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) may feel it to be, does not begin to deal with what the Government identified as its main objective and thrust, jobs, jobs, and more jobs.
January 28, 1985

In fact, let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, why this legislation runs counter to the avowed intents of the Government. It runs counter-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Government House Leader)
speechtext: In your mind.

No, not in my mind but in point of fact. It runs counter to what the Government has said.
You remember as I remember, Sir, that when the Prime Minister was first seeking the leadership of his Party and subsequently when he was seeking the office of the Prime Minister, he identified, quite justifiably and rightly so, that the main problem facing the country was jobs, jobs, and more jobs. I am not even paraphrasing him but am quoting him verbatim.
Let me draw to your attention, Sir, a situation that has arisen in the City of Hamilton that directly touches upon this legislation. I am sure all Hon. Members are familiar with the corporation known as United Technologies. United Technologies has a very bad habit which it developed over many years in many parts of the world. United Technologies acquires companies, then systematically moves to reduce their effectiveness and ultimately closes those companies. I am sure that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps) is familiar with what I am about to say.
Some years ago, United Technologies was able to purchase Otis Elevator. As a result of its program of closure, it has effectively reduced the opportunity for many hundreds of people from the City of Hamilton to hold down viable occupations.
Every day I come across people who are in their late forties and early fifties, and I am sure my colleague from Hamilton East does as well, who have worked all or most of their adult lives for Otis Elevator. These people did not want United Technologies to take them over. They did not expect that as a result of United Technologies having made substantial commitments, it would move to close the plant and disburse its operations around the world. They did not expect that it would undermine their security and ability to provide for their families. Yet that is exactly what happened.
This is an example of a major corporation moving into Canada with money to invest, purchasing a viable enterprise and then deciding to close it. This operation was closed not because it was not a working operation, not because it did not produce high technology products, not because the product was not recognized as a world leader in its field, but because that particular company decided, for whatever balance sheet reasons it may have had, that it would rather produce some if not all of its products either in the United States or in West Germany.
Is that the kind of investment Tory Members want? Is that what we are about to encourage? Is that an example of what we anticipate will be the great benefit we will derive from the investment that will flow into Canada when we eliminate the review process? If it is, I can cite chapter and verse of other similar situations that have arisen over the course of the last
Adjournment Motion
five or six years. These situations have occurred in spite of the review process.
I say that during its lifetime the review process was inadequate. Instead of eliminating it, we should be strengthening it. The review process should have required that certain commitments, once made, were lived up to. The review process should have required that if a corporation were allowed to take over a major part of Canada's economy, then the very least we could expect in return is that people in Canada would receive jobs. However, that did not happen.
Given that years ago this country was an open field in which one could buy whatever was desired with whatever currency from wherever one came and given that we found over a long period of time that that worked to our detriment and that we needed a process for protecting ourselves against unfair purchasing and closures of our major operations, I would have anticipated that this Government would have recognized that the road to prosperity lay not in returning to those days which resulted in FIR A but rather in looking at the FIR A operation, streamlining it in those areas which required streamlining and toughening its provisions in those areas which required toughening.
The Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) knows, as I know, that over the years, in spite of extracting promises from the majority of those who took over major operations in Canada, we were never able or willing to follow up and require that they performed according to how they said they would in their promises. That was the weakness of FIRA. That is where the process should have been changed.
As a young friend said to me, perhaps it would be more advantageous if we addressed ourselves to the question which is uppermost in the minds of 1.5 million or two million Canadians, that is, where they will find work this year, not five years or ten years from now. This Government certainly is not moving to provide any answer to that question.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext:
It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 45, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy)-Research-Cancellation of proposed Winnipeg Manufacturing Research Centre, (b) Government policy on consultation; the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker)-Environmental Affairs-Proposed weather service information charge, (b) Method of implementation; the Hon.

January 28, 1985
Investment Canada Act
Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps)-Status of Women-Government's position, (b) Election campaign statement.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Stevens that Bill C-15, an Act respecting investment in Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Regional Development; and on the motion of Mrs. Tardif (Charlesbourg) (p. 1708).

Mr. Speaker, I would like to join in the comments made not only by my colleagues of the Liberal Party, but also by the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans).
After a few days of absence to attend the Ontario Progressive Conservative Leadership Convention, the result of which has made me extremely happy, I was surpprised to find out upon my return that this Government has introduced some kind of closure in a debate on a tremendously significant issue for the Canadian people.
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my party, I must say that I am extremely surprised that this Government, which, last September 4, succeeded in electing an unprecedented 211 Members to Parliament, cannot find in its ranks anyone ready to speak on foreign investments in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, it is true the Liberal Party has been decimated. We now have 40 Members in this House and the NDP has 30. Nevertheless, to meet the needs of our constituents, Members of both parties have addressed the problems raised by the legislation introduced by this Government. As for the Government majority, its Members sit in silence.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to know whether the Conservatives have taken position for or against anything? They certainly have not taken position on the Bill respecting investment which was introduced by this Government.
Mr. Speaker, 1 am surprised that the Conservative Members from my region of Hamilton are not rising to speak about foreign investment in Canada. We all know that, in Hamilton, the iron ore industry as represented by the Steel Company and Dofasco is at the forefront of Canadian industries, which shows the Canadian people that we can be a world leader when we want.
Mr. Speaker, putting aside the question of foreign investment for a while, we can see that this Bill does not mention investments by Canadians. In this case, how can we help businesses like the Steel Company, how can we help Dominion Foundries so that everyone can benefit from their investments? Let us speak about investments by Canadians. We can compete with anyone. This is already happening in the steel
industry. We know that we Canadians are the best in the world. This is why the Americans would like to freeze iron imports to the United States. Mr. Speaker, I really cannot understand why the Conservative Members of Parliament are not interested either in foreign investment in Canada or in Canadian investment abroad.
Mr. Speaker, we have at least four years before us in view of the unprecedented majority of the Government. Therefore, how can we consider too long two or three weeks of debate for a bill which the Government knows to be this important? I would have thought that every member of each party would rise to speak either to support, to defend or to oppose this legislation. But I see that they are not interested in investments and do not see it as the key which can open not only the doors of our Canadian economy, but also international markets for Canadians. Mr. Speaker, this is the question that this Parliament, this Government and this Minister should ask if they want new markets for Canadians, because it is certain that it is not by looking only at investments in Canada that we can improve our economy for Canadians. It is obvious that our main task is to increase Canadian markets abroad. Mr. Speaker, in this type of closure, and in this-

We have seen a cloak and closure operation with respect to the Investment Canada Bill. I wonder why we have not heard from government Members. I invite government Members from the Hamilton area to stand in the House and indicate if they are in favour of the Bill.
There are 40 Liberal Members. We sit on numerous committees. We are here to defend not only the rights of our constituents, but the rights of all Canadians on the major issues of the day. There were 211 Conservatives elected in an unprecedented majority last September, but the Government cannot muster the manpower to speak to a Bill which will affect the livelihoods, the jobs and the future of all Canadians.
We have already spoken on that.

The Hon. Member for Mississauga South says that Conservatives have already spoken on it. I would suggest that there has not been a Conservative in the Hamilton area who has spoken to this issue. I invite them to put their positions on the record. A closure motion introduced in the early stages of a Parliament-
Let's vote.

Mr. Speaker, I am afraid that the Hon. Member's eye is not the only thing that is closed today. The issue is not only one of a full and open discussion, including amendments to this Bill which I have named "Abandon Canada'', but it is also one that requires the contribution of all Members of the House. An extremely dangerous precedent has been set by the Parliamentary Secretary who introduced a motion which effectively muzzles the few representatives which we have in Opposition preventing them from putting outlining,
January 28, 1985

underlining and promoting the concerns and interests of Canadians.
I would have thought that with 211 government Members- many of whom are seeking opportunities to do something because they do not have a defined job in the Government as a Parliamentary Secretary or Minister-they would have looked for opportunities to defend the interests of their constituents. Elowever, not only do governdment Members stand by, muzzled and mum, when they have the opportunity to speak on the issue of Investment Canada, but the Government, through the auspices of the Parliamentary Secretary, who presumably is acting with the full consent of the Prime Minister and the Cabinet, brings closure to a motion at the very earliest stage of this session of Parliament. That is a very dangerous precedent and one about which I should think the Canadian people must be concerned and, indeed, outraged.
We do not have great numbers here on the opposition side of the House. We know that with only 40 Hon. Members, we must cover committees and Private Members' Business and we must speak on a number of issues. But it seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that given the small numbers on the opposition side of the House, and given the Government's large majority mandate, this Government does not need closure. It should give Hon. Members an opportunity to exercise their mental acuity and allow them to get up to speak to the people of Canada about what they think this Bill is going to do for the Canadian people. Putting their words on the record will hold those same Hon. Members accountable.
What about jobs for people, for a change?

The Hon. Member for Mississauga South asks about jobs. As a matter of fact, if the pretended Minister, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South, had his ears and eyes open, he would know that one of the glaring omissions in this particular Bill is the fact that there is nothing which addresses the issue of Canadian investment in the international market. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we have to open our eyes to the world and to the fact that the Canadian economy, in order to compete on an international basis, will have to take a lesson from the steel industry of Canada. That industry has competed all over the world and deserves not our derision, not our laughs and jokes in the House of Commons, but our full support in the way of legislation and the expansion of a Bill which would allow Canadians to compete in the international marketplace. We do not have to play second fiddle or take second place to the Americans, Mr. Speaker. We can compete and we will compete. It is about time the Government took the lid off this closure motion, allowed Hon. Members in the Opposition to make some amendments which would improve this Bill, and let the Canadian people, for once, flex their muscles in the economic market.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a sad heart that I stand to speak on the amendment which was introduced by an Hon. Member for whom I have had
Investment Canada Act
some respect since I have returned to this House, namely, the Hon. Member for Charlesbourg (Mrs. Tardif).
I have spent eight years here in the House of Commons, from 1972 to 1980, and when the Liberals were in government, there were many occasions on which they tried to muzzle the Opposition. At that time the Conservatives were sitting as the Official Opposition, and I can remember the cries of anger and pain and the accusations that the Government was attempting to muzzle Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition. Lo and behold, Mr. Speaker, now that those Hon. Members are sitting on the government side of the House, they are performing in exactly the same arrogant and fatuous manner as the Liberals did when they sat on the government side.
This amendment, which in effect closes off debate on this very important national issue of foreign investment, is certainly illogical. When I was speaking with the Hon. Member for Charlesbourg earlier, she asked me what exactly it is that the Opposition is opposed to. She said, "I would like to know what it is you oppose in Bill C-15".

First, we have the opening of the country to foreign investment without any meaningful criteria as to whether or not that investment ought to benefit Canadians. We need to see this along with changes in respect of environmental policy where the Government has declared, in the interests of bettering the investment climate and reducing the deficit, that it will not be as concerned as it used to be about what factories, plants and various other forms of economic activity are putting into our
lakes, rivers, air, soil or whatever. This is another signal to the investment community that Canada is a good place in which to invest because it does not care as much about the environment as it used to.

["Mr. Speaker, I would like to commend the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) for the concern that he has expressed about the entrenchment of property rights in the Constitution. This is a matter in which many Canadians are interested. It is for that reason, however, that I must agree that Private Members' Hour is not the appropriate forum for resolving this matter.
I, no less than my colleagues, am sympathetic in principle to the entrenchment of property rights in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. These rights are deserving of the protection they can be afforded by entrenchment in the Constitution. By entrenching property rights in the Constitution we would do two things. First, we would be making a statement about the importance of property rights and the value they hold for ordinary Canadians. Second, we would at the same time be providing Canadians with legal rights enforceable in our courts of law. Because the Charter of Rights and Freedoms is the supreme law of the land, these rights will prevail over laws enacted by Government where these laws infringe upon the enjoyment of the rights. The importance of these rights should therefore not be underestimated.
We in the Progressive Conservative Party do not underestimate the importance of entrenching property rights. Hon. Members have heard my colleagues speak of the continuing support of the Progressive Conservative Party for the entrenchment of property rights. This support was reiterated during the recent election campaign. During the campaign, in response to questions about this matter, the Conservative Party provided the following answer:
A Progressive Conservative Government will consult with the provinces with a view to amending the constitution to recognize property rights in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, while ensuring that any such amendment does not adversely affect other bona fide rights of individuals (for example, in family law). We believe that the exercise of this right has been instrumental in the building of Canada and is a principle valued by the great majority of Canadians. As you know, the right to enjoyment of property is recognized in the Canadian Bill of Rights. We believe it should be part of our constitution.
I think this statement is a good indication of the depth of our commitment to the entrenchment of property rights.", 'January 28, 1985
Adjournment Debate
The historical importance of property rights in our society is clear. It can be traced back as far as the Magna Carta in 1215. The development of property rights is linked with the development of our democratic institutions. This link was noted by the Hon. Member for Richmond-South Delta, (Mr. Siddon), who is now the Minister of State for Science and Technology, on the occasion of a motion to entrench property rights in the Constitution which was brought forward by the Progressive Conservative Party in 1983. The Hon. Member said, as reported at page 24,999 of Hansard for April 29, 1983.
If we go back in history we find that not only the right to own and enjoy property is fundamental to Canadian history. As the Hon. Member for Pro-vencher pointed out, it goes back to the time of King John, the Magna Carta and the constant struggle through history, which went hand in hand with the evolution of the parliamentary system and with the evolution of property rights and individual rights as a means of escape from monarchism, feudalism and the baronial entitlements, previous systems under which some citizens had many more rights, powers and privileges than others.']
