subtopic: CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 ADVISABILITY OF AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE PROPERTY RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say first that I appreciate the commitment which the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) has to the entrenchment of property rights in our Constitution. At the same time, I would argue strenuously that Private Members' Hour is not an appropriate forum for resolving matters of such constitutional, economic and social significance. We simply lack the time and the collective capacity to assess and deal with complex constitutional initiatives in the span of time available to us. Our debate does, however, enable us to touch on some of the issues and to get a better idea of what may be involved in entrenching property rights in the Constitution.
I would like to express my personal support in principle for the entrenchment of protection for property rights in the Constitution. Property rights are, in my opinion, fundamental to our way of life. Property rights are basic civil rights that enable us to carry on our lives without having to depend on the state for sustenance. They are the basis of our right to carry on and profit from business activities. They allow us to acquire all those things we need and want in our daily lives. The point of property rights, as with the other rights and freedoms which have received constitutional protection, is to afford us a measure of independence from government; some degree of protection against well-meant, but perhaps unnecessary, state interference.
The entrenchment of property rights in the Constitution would be a symbol to ordinary Canadians of the enduring importance of such rights in Canada. It would also be a symbol of their right to own and enjoy property without arbitrary or ill-considered interference by government. The importance of such symbols should not be underestimated. The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, in addition to providing legal remedies for the violation of the rights and
Constitution Act, 1982
freedoms set out in the Charter, is a symbolic document. It is a symbol to Canadians, and it is a symbol that we can hold out to the world, especially to countries where these rights and freedoms and, in particular, property rights do not exist.
Many Canadians left their homes in other countries so that they could enjoy the rights and freedoms which we take for granted in Canada. They are vigilant about maintaining these rights and freedoms. They have worked hard to build families, homes and businesses, and to contribute to the development of Canada, and they rightfully expect that the things they have worked so hard for will be protected. They recognize that an important way of securing this protection is by entrenching property rights in the Constitution.
At the same time, I wish to acknowledge that there are important societal interests which require governments to enact laws that affect property rights. These interests must be taken into account. The provinces have acted to protect the interests of women arising out of family relationships. In recognition of the contribution of women in the family relationship, important family law reforms have been made to provide for the division of family assets, regardless of the apparent legal title, upon mariage breakdown.
The Supreme Court of Canada has, within the last few days, agreed to consider the rights of common law spouses, on the termination of a long-standing spousal relationship, in the Sorochan case. What would the entrenchment of property rights in the Constitution portend for the evolution of such a re-evaluation of common law property tenets by reference to changed societal standards? We simply do not know, and an abstract and unqualified entrenchment of property rights does not permit us to predict the outcome of this balancing of important societal values.
More generally, societal interests are reflected in the multitude of laws which in one way or another affect property rights. The provinces have sought assurances that their right to enact such laws will not be unreasonably restricted. We should note that only two provinces have passed resolutions supporting the entrenchment of property rights. No other provinces have passed such resolutions. They are concerned about the effect that constitutional protection for the enjoyment of property rights might have on their authority to enact a wide variety of regulatory laws. Provincial laws affecting property rights include such basic incidents of an orderly society as land use planning and municipal laws, laws concerning the acquisition and disposition of real and personal property, construction lien laws, environmental laws, and expropriation laws. This is by no means an exhaustive list. When one considers the scope and extent of existing provincial regulation of property, one can understand something of the apprehension which the provinces have with respect to entrenching the enjoyment of property rights.
The concerns of the provinces are reflected in a unanimous resolution of the Council of the Canadian Bar Association of Ontario. That resolution, as it was reported at page 1 of the June 1984 edition of "Briefly Speaking", the monthly newslet-

January 28, 1985
Constitution Act, 1982
ter of the Canadian Bar Association-Ontario, reads as follows:
Various provincial governments have indicated their intentions to seek entrenchment of property rights in the Constitution;
1 take it that the authors of this resolution are referring to the resolutions of the Legislatures of British Columbia and New Brunswick in support of the entrenchment of property rights. The resolution continues:
And whereas property rights entrenchment may affect environmental, resource, land use planning, municipal and real property laws; And Whereas very limited study of how entrenchment may affect these laws has occurred; And whereas the federal Minister of Environment and Ontario Minister of the Environment have both requested that the CBA/CBAO undertake such a study; now therefore be it resolved that CBAO strike a committee to study how property rights entrenchment may affect matters including environmental, resource, land use planning, municipal and real property laws for a report to Council-
It is evident that the provinces have sincere concerns about the entrenchment of property rights. These concerns cannot be ignored, and it is clear that the substantive resolution of these issues is essential to the extension of constitutional protection for property rights.
The legitimacy of provincial concern is underlined by the fact that the Constitution gives the provinces a primary role in making laws in relation to property. Section 92(13) of the Constitution Act, 1867 provides that each province may exclusively make laws with respect to "Property and Civil Rights in the province". Other provisions of Section 92 further extend the powers of the provinces to enact laws affecting property rights. In the exercise of these powers the provinces have made laws which, as I noted earlier, affect property rights in many respects. The provinces have also, as they are entitled to do, delegated to municipal bodies the power to make such laws.
In the interests of community planning, and public health and safety, the provinces have enacted land use planning laws and have enabled municipalities to pass zoning laws, building codes and health and safety regulations. Land use planning and zoning laws may regulate or restrict the development and use of land to ensure that these serve the community interest. For example, residential areas may be protected from industries incompatible with residential use. Building codes ensure that our homes and offices are built to meet proper and safe engineering and design standards. Safety regulations ensure that buildings are adequately designed and equipped to allow us to deal with emergencies such as fire. Health regulations ensure that our public facilities are sanitary and ensure that public health conditions are consistent with human habitation.
Provincial laws have been enacted to protect the environment. They control industrial land uses which might create pollution through industrial wastes and emissions. Provincial laws protect our cultural heritage as well as our natural heritage. They do so by preserving historic sites and other precious assets of our cultural heritage.
In addition to regulating the use of property, the provinces also regulate the process of acquisition and disposition of real property such as land and personal property such as automobiles. In any given property, there may be several interests held
by different people. For instance, with respect to a given piece of real estate there may be, for example, the interests of the registered owner, a first mortgagee and subsequent mortgagees and the holder of an easement. In addition, it is possible for creditors to obtain a lien against the land or to register a judgment against the land. The provinces have created laws for the orderly creation, transfer and disposition of these interests. These laws govern the interaction of all these interests and establish priorities. They also ensure that persons dealing with real property can ensure that they are getting that for which they contracted. Similar laws apply to personal property.
It is sometimes necessary when it is in the public interest to expropriate property for important public purposes. The law allows for the expropriation of land for public highways or public utilities with reasonable compensation to the landowners affected. The federal government, as much as the provinces, needs to preserve this power while recognizing the need for adequate safeguards for property owners.
As you can see by my examples, Mr. Speaker, there are a wide range of areas in which the provinces have made laws affecting property or the enjoyment of property. In these are reflected a variety of vital societal interests which the provinces protect in the public interest. They are concerned, however, that provincial laws will be vunerable to attack if property rights are entrenched in the Constitution. It is not that the provinces wish to insulate their legislation from standards of fairness, far from it.
The provinces have attempted to balance societal interests against individual property rights by providing built in protections for property rights. Many provincial laws which purport to affect some sort of property right provide procedural as well as substantive protections for such rights. In many cases, citizens have a right to a fair hearing, a right to present their side of the case, and a right to appeal. Many of these procedural protections are also provided at common law by the rules of natural justice. Substantive protections also exist in provincial laws. For example, expropriation laws generally allow the expropriation of property only for important public purposes where no alternative course is available and only with reasonable compensation.
The provinces do not appear to be concerned so much about the entrenchment of procedural protections for property rights as they are about any action which might allow the courts to become arbiters of what is or is not acceptable government policy for laws affecting property rights. The provinces wish to have the assurance that property rights guarantees will not be used to strike down laws protecting important societal interests.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we should be taking steps to allay as much as possible the concerns of the provinces and to seek a consensus, if possible, on the entrenchment of property rights. Our efforts would, of course, be premised on our support in principle for the entrenchment of property
January 28, 1985

rights, subject to our commitment made during the election campaign that this could only be accomplished without prejudice to women's interests.
The provinces and other interested parties should be given a reasonable opportunity to give this matter their fullest consideration and to voice their views. A co-operative approach with respect to the entrenchment of property rights will avoid unnecessary obstacles and will smooth the road to constitutional change. Constitutional change is not a unilateral process. It requires, in this case, the support of at least seven provinces.
While I have so far focused on the concerns of the provinces, a property rights amendment would also have ramifications for the federal Government. The federal Government has also passed a multitude of laws affecting property rights. These include, for example, copyright laws, environmental laws, land use laws, and laws dealing with the exploitation of our natural resources. These laws, no less than provincial laws, serve important societal interests. We should be clear about the effect that the entrenchment of property rights would have on these laws.
Like most Canadians, I recognize that the pressing issues of the day are economic. The Government is committed to restoring the economy, to encouraging business and to putting Canadians back to work. These are, for Canadians, the top priorities. We understand that the process of constitutional change takes time and work but we know it will receive due consideration.
Our support for the entrenchment of property rights is no less firm for wanting to ensure that any constitutional amendment would not be prejudicial to the interests of women and to other important societal interests. The amendment of the Constitution, however, is not a matter that should be taken lightly. The potential consequences of an amendment must be carefully assessed because undesirable consequences cannot be easily remedied once the amendment has been made. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, the entrenchment of property rights deserves our careful and considered analysis.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to this motion today on behalf of the New Democratic Party. Any time that there is a motion to create our first amendment to the Constitution, it is a very serious business. The Government is being told that it would be a good idea to introduce an amendment to the Constitution. As has been stated by the Hon. Member who just spoke, a process for doing so is now in place and it is very straightforward. It simply requires the approval of seven provinces and the Government of Canada to make such a constitutional change which would in effect transfer the jurisdiction over the rights of property and their enforcement from the provincial to the federal level.
I realize that there is a Progressive Conservative Government at the federal level and that there are at least seven provinces in this country that are also run by Progressive
Constitution Act, 1982
Conservative Governments. I believe, therefore, that any such process would move along quickly and smoothly and that we would see a motion for such constitutional amendment before the House very soon.
As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, the provinces and the federal Government must hold discussions to bring about such an agreement. They would make proposals to make constitutional change which, upon the agreement of the seven provinces and the federal Government, would then be presented to the House of Commons for discussion and debate. The whole process would then be transferred to a committee, at which time ordinary Canadians could have input. At that time, the provinces and the federal Government would already have had their discussions.
As I understand it, this matter did come up during the election and was apparently one of the planks of the Conservative Party platform. I am a little confused as to why it is necessary to keep reminding the Government of one of its promises by putting this motion before it.
Before we get too far into this process for change, I believe there are a number of questions that should be asked and a number of answers that should be provided. First, I would argue that property rights have been well taken care of within the provincial sphere, with perhaps a few exceptions which could be considered minor within the scheme of things. When I ask myself when property rights have been abused or not properly upheld on the part of Canadians, not very many instances come to mind. That is one of the first questions I ask myself when I talk about a constitutional amendment. I can think of a few examples of such abuse, one being the confiscation of the property of Japanese-Canadians during the last war. At about the same time, the padlock laws were instituted in Quebec and the Jehovah's Witnesses were not granted the right to use their halls and churches. However, I would point out that even with the Constitution and with the right of property being moved from federal to provincial jurisdiction, both of those circumstances would probably have occurred whether or not there were property rights in the federal Constitution. I contend that what we had in the case of Japanese-Canadians was a very emotionally charged period of time. We were at war with another racial group. What happened to the Japanese-Canadians had nothing to do with property, but probably had everything to do with the racial attitude toward those people at that time. I am from a Germanic background and our property was not confiscated during the First or Second World Wars. My grandparents, who were Canadian citizens, well before the First World War, went to visit their parents inthe United States and were prohibited from returning in the fall of 1914 because of the outbreak of war. However, their property was not seized. They had to spend the next 4.5 years in the United States because the Canadian Government would not permit them to return, even though they were citizens. But their property was not seized. Therefore, I contend that the Japanese-Canadian situation would probably have happened whether or not there had been a guarantee of property rights.

Constitution Act, 1982
Similarly but for different reasons, the Jehovah's Witnesses were locked out of their properties, essentially for religious reasons. Both racial and religious discrimination are now prohibited under the Constitution, but we have yet to discover whether that constitutional strength would be adequate to stop such things happening in the future. Perhaps we would be well advised not to rush into changing the constitutional responsibility from provincial to federal jurisdiction until it is discovered whether in fact the federal jurisdiction could be effective in dealing with these very real problems of racial and religious discrimination which occurred in the past.
There is some indication from the provinces that they are not in a hurry to make that change. The Province of Alberta has a property rights contract with its citizens, but it is still possible in Alberta, if the property is on the route to a pipeline, power line or telephone line, that the property can be just as easily seized as a right of way for public use, as it is in provinces which do not have guaranteed property rights. On the surface it is difficult to find an advantage in that particular province which has property rights. I would also remind the House that Alberta is one province which has been very vociferous in opposing any move to change property rights from provincial to federal jurisdiction. It would be an important necessity for that province to go along with such a change as it is one of the seven provinces which would be required to agree to such a constitutional change. Being from the same political stripe as the federal Government, one would think that Alberta would be among the first on the bandwagon to go along with this proposal.
There is some question as to the kind of rights which will be guaranteed. It is generally agreed by all that property is land. However, when we get beyond houses, factories, businesses, barns and that sort of thing, we get into a fuzzy area as to what is property. I believe there is general agreement that bonds and mortgages are forms of property, but the question arises in the case of a mortgage as to which property interest takes precedence. Will that be spelled out in the Constitution? If there is a disagreement as to whether the terms of a mortgage are being met, does the bank get precedence over the man or woman who is trying to make the payments?
We could look at contracts. Is an insurance policy property? If it is, is a labour contract not also a form of property? If that is the case, is it then possible for workers who have a labour contract with a factory to be put out of the factory either in the form of lock-out or lay-off? How many rights are included in the contract, if it is indeed property?
Whose property takes precedence? For example, we could talk about environmental concerns. Do we shrug off the pollution which our own generation is creating because it will not hurt us, but will put into jeopardy future generations by creating acid rain which kills our lakes, trees and soil? Does a property resolution change any of those questions? How would having property rights written into the Constitution provide guarantees for future generations for a usable environment, for land which will grow crops, for land which will produce trees
and for lakes which will produce fish? I doubt if it makes any difference. I believe the inclusion of property rights in the Constitution makes no difference to the groups of people which I have mentioned.
We must recognize that the property rights which we have in Canada have come down to us through British common law and that those of us who have property hold it in right of fee simple from the Crown. The rights which we have are clearly stated in the title, as to the minerals above and below the ground, whether we must grant access to public utilities, or whether we must provide a road crossing in the property. The title also describes the liens and mortgages which exist against the property. However, the title also bears some responsibility. We must pay the taxes, and often it requires us to keep the property in good order, depending on the community in which it is found. If the property is in a farming community, the owner must guard against noxious weeds. The owner could be obligated to keep a building from going into disrepair. Factories cannot be built in residential areas. There are numerous things an owner cannot do with property because of community requirements. The rights which the owner has are only those rights which are allowed after consideration of the community and consideration of the requirements of the Crown.
We have got along with this system, Mr. Speaker, for quite a few hundred years. I have not heard anyone previously in this debate outline any large shortcomings in this system. So I ask Hon. Members of the House very simply and clearly, if there are no problems with the existing system, why should we change it? Why take the right of property away from the provinces and enshrine it under federal jurisdiction? Particularly when there are so many different kinds of interests at stake in different parts of the country, does it make sense to centralize this particular right? What does it do for the right of Prince Edward Island to decide that it should not have a large influx of foreign ownership of its prime recreation land? Is it so wrong that Prince Edward Island should make certain that people who have access to its lovely beaches are Islanders, or at least Canadians? Is that not infringing upon the right of the person, who has the money to pay for such a beach, to own it, whether he lives in Hong Kong or in Bonn? Those are some questions which have been dealt with in that particular province and it has said, "No, we have first right to those beaches".
Similarly, in British Columbia there is a question of what sort of policy should apply to the ownership of the very limited amount of farm land there. That province has determined that there should be some restrictions on who owns farm land. Only farmers may own farm land, and it must be used for agricultural purposes. If we had a guarantee of property rights in the Constitution, would British Columbia still have that right or would whoever had the money to buy that farm land be permitted to do whatever he chose with it? What would be the implications to future generations of British Columbians who were looking for agricultural production and found that they were not able to provide a lot of their own food themselves?

What about the land of the Indian and the Inuit in this kind of constitution amendment? As you know, Mr. Speaker, the Crown, on behalf of Canada, took over those lands through treaty. The Indians were not really aware of that fact but that is what the Crown did. Then, as I interpret it, the Crown transferred a great many of the rights to resources and jurisdiction over the property to the provinces, and now the Indian and Inuit are attempting to negotiate with the federal Government to make certain that with respect to the treaties, and in those areas where there are still no treaties, there is an understanding that there are some rights that the original people have, which are retained rights, even though a treaty has been signed. And we get into the question of whether game is property for the Inuit and the Indians. It is a very contentious question which has not been properly dealt with. Certainly, it has not been adequately answered by deciding to change property rights from provincial back to federal jurisdiction.
In closing, I would like to point out once again that the process is quite clear now that we have an amending formula for the Constitution. The Government in this case, if it is interested in initiating such a discussion, can and should initiate such a discussion with the provinces, then the words which have been agreed to can be brought to this House. We will then look at that agreement and decide whether to accept it or oppose it. It will go to the committee where all Canadians can have a chance to decide whether it is good or bad for them as Canadians. If the resolution passes, the amendment to the Constitution, some of the provinces would still have the option of opting out at five-year intervals. So we may see the very real possibility that even with an amendment, a great many if not all of the provinces would find themselves opting out.
My main point, Mr. Speaker, is that I have great difficulty in seeing an advantage to a radical change to the Constitution when there have been no reasons set forth as to what advantage there will be for us as Canadians. I have not seen any of that in this debate thus far. I hope that future speakers will point those things out, if they are really serious about amending the Constitution in such a manner.

The other reason that I think the Charter is not a protection is that it is written the wrong way. It is written from the wrong perspective. At least the U.S. Bill of Rights is written from the perspective of people limiting the power of government. The Canadian Charter of Rights is the government extending a list of rights to the people. That is wrong. It is an underlying weakness of our Charter.
I am saying to the Hon. Member that there are problems and that a charter is not necessarily going to protect us. Even though we include this in the Charter it will not necessarily protect us. However, we do have the Charter and we have to live with it. Therefore, let us take those realistic items that the Canadian people believe ought to be included and list them in that Charter. The Member says that there are no problems with the existing system. I have said already that the existing system is not the one we are accustomed to. We are in a transitional period from common law to constitutional law. We are moving into a new regime. We are in kind of amorphous state at this point.
We have historically been an agrarian nation with fairly small government. In the last couple of decades we have become more populated and certainly more cosmopolitan. We now have a Government that is growing and has grown for the last couple of decades. In my view the purpose of the Charter ought not to be so much to protect us from each other, but to protect us from the Government. That was the entire purpose of the U.S. Bill of Rights; to protect people from an ominous, overriding and bullying government. If the Charter is going to function in any logical and responsible way, that is what it ought to do for us. The Canadian Government is growing year by year. It certainly has done so in the last two decades. Canadian citizens need to feel that there is a limitation upon Government, that it cannot willy-nilly encroach upon the rights of citizens.
I think it is important that in the historical experience of western countries the freedom and right to own property is integrally involved with political freedom. It is not that way around the world. I know there are regimes where that is not the case. In Africa, for example, there is a communal system. In western countries it is pretty well unanimously true that when you have the right to own property you also have political freedom because you can always be independent and make it on your own. In those countries where property has
Constitution Act, 1982
been taken away from the people, there is no political freedom. That is a fairly uniform experience in western countries.
The way to make people insecure is to take away their ability to look after themselves. They have no guarantee of being able to look after themselves if they do not have their own property. That is certainly the case in the eastern European countries.
It is important that we urge the Government that the inalienable and undeniable right to own property be entrenched, not to protect us from each other, but to protect us from a Government that becomes insensitive, loses its touch with people, and thinks it has its own reason for being. I commend the Member for Mississauga South for bringing this motion forward. I hope that we will soon see the day when these rights will be entrenched in our Constitution.

speechtext: Is the House ready for the question?

subtopic: CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 ADVISABILITY OF AMENDMENT TO INCLUDE PROPERTY RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to commend the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) for the concern that he has expressed about the entrenchment of property rights in the Constitution. This is a matter in which many Canadians are interested. It is for that reason, however, that I must agree that Private Members' Hour is not the appropriate forum for resolving this matter.
I, no less than my colleagues, am sympathetic in principle to the entrenchment of property rights in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. These rights are deserving of the protection they can be afforded by entrenchment in the Constitution. By entrenching property rights in the Constitution we would do two things. First, we would be making a statement about the importance of property rights and the value they hold for ordinary Canadians. Second, we would at the same time be providing Canadians with legal rights enforceable in our courts of law. Because the Charter of Rights and Freedoms is the supreme law of the land, these rights will prevail over laws enacted by Government where these laws infringe upon the enjoyment of the rights. The importance of these rights should therefore not be underestimated.
We in the Progressive Conservative Party do not underestimate the importance of entrenching property rights. Hon. Members have heard my colleagues speak of the continuing support of the Progressive Conservative Party for the entrenchment of property rights. This support was reiterated during the recent election campaign. During the campaign, in response to questions about this matter, the Conservative Party provided the following answer:
A Progressive Conservative Government will consult with the provinces with a view to amending the constitution to recognize property rights in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, while ensuring that any such amendment does not adversely affect other bona fide rights of individuals (for example, in family law). We believe that the exercise of this right has been instrumental in the building of Canada and is a principle valued by the great majority of Canadians. As you know, the right to enjoyment of property is recognized in the Canadian Bill of Rights. We believe it should be part of our constitution.
I think this statement is a good indication of the depth of our commitment to the entrenchment of property rights.

January 28, 1985
Adjournment Debate
The historical importance of property rights in our society is clear. It can be traced back as far as the Magna Carta in 1215. The development of property rights is linked with the development of our democratic institutions. This link was noted by the Hon. Member for Richmond-South Delta, (Mr. Siddon), who is now the Minister of State for Science and Technology, on the occasion of a motion to entrench property rights in the Constitution which was brought forward by the Progressive Conservative Party in 1983. The Hon. Member said, as reported at page 24,999 of Hansard for April 29, 1983.
If we go back in history we find that not only the right to own and enjoy property is fundamental to Canadian history. As the Hon. Member for Pro-vencher pointed out, it goes back to the time of King John, the Magna Carta and the constant struggle through history, which went hand in hand with the evolution of the parliamentary system and with the evolution of property rights and individual rights as a means of escape from monarchism, feudalism and the baronial entitlements, previous systems under which some citizens had many more rights, powers and privileges than others.

subtopic: RESEARCH-CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED WINNIPEG MANUFACTURING RESEARCH CENTRE. (B) GOVERNMENT POLICY ON CONSULTATION
RESEARCH-CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED WINNIPEG MANUFACTURING RESEARCH CENTRE. (B) GOVERNMENT POLICY ON CONSULTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak on the adjournment motion with respect to a question I raised in the House on November 14, but which has a currency that surpasses the elapse of time because it is a matter that is still of very important consequences for the economic development of this country and the economic growth of my own region of Manitoba.
Last week I had the opportunity to present a petition in the House which was signed by over 1,000 residents of the City of Winnipeg asking the federal Government once again to reconsider its decision to close and cut back the major development of the National Research Industrial Technology Laboratory in Winnipeg. I think that by this time the reasons for that are well known, but what is not so clear is the fact that this particular development met every single criteria that was put forward in the statement by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson).
What I could not determine during the Question Period is why a project that met the test of consultation, met the test of research and development, that met the test of new economic
growth and development in fact was rejected by the Tory Government.
A brief history might just recall to members' minds what took place. The NRC laboratory was based upon consultation that had gone on for over four years between business, labour, universities, the provincial Government and the federal Government. The objective of that centre was to establish in western Canada an industrial technology laboratory that would provide a stimulus for new manufacturing technology for all of Canada. It would give us the capacity and ability to compete internationally to sell our products abroad and help in particular our small business people to develop new industrial techniques to meet overseas competition.
Furthermore, it was located in a western Canadian city to make sure that the benefits of high technology were not concentrated in just one or two regions of Canada, but in fact shared and distributed equally across Canada.
Furthermore, it was part and parcel of the major downtown development program that would bring new workers into that downtown area and therefore enhance the over-all economic growth of that region. The building was already under construction. The research people had been hired. They were already in Winnipeg undertaking research at the university.
What is more important, over four major companies, some of which were from California in the United States and other places, had decided to locate brand new manufacturing facilities in Winnipeg as a result of the decision, to locate the laboratory in that city. This would have provided new jobs for Canada. It would have provided new manufacturing technology for Canada and would have provided a major stimulus for the growth of Manitoba. It would have given hope to young people coming out of our universities and training colleges that there was a place to go. Instead, the Government cancelled the project.
To the credit of people in Manitoba, they have not given up on that. They have not accepted that decision. A number of organizations, the university, the Chamber of Commerce and a coalition of citizens continue to make representations. As their Member of Parliament, I am here once again to make that representation and have the Government once again rethink the project, come to its senses and recognize that the cancellation of that project did nothing but hurt Manitoba, Winnipeg and the country.
I would suggest to members, as I have tried during Question Period, that, if the Government is so wedded to its notion that the federal Government should not be totally committed to paying for the National Research centre, it should at least accept the proposal that we establish research co-op. I suggest that we work out an arrangement whereby the universities, the business community and the governments would share responsibility for that lab and its development and projection and share responsibilty for developing an economic plan for that region growing out of the institute's research facility. On the basis of the Government's own argument for consultation and co-operation, surely it could at least accept the proposal which
January 28, 1985

is being made by the broad community of the Province of Manitoba representing all sectors.
Time is of essence. The longer the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Siddon) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) drag out the decision and the longer they keep things hanging, the more we will lose those businesses which were planning to locate there, the more we will lose the scientists and engineers who came to Winnipeg to work in that laboratory, and the more we will lose the opportunity for young people to plan their careers in relation to the facilities which the laboratory would have stimulated.
Not only is my intervention at this time a plea for the Government to respond to the proposals for a research co-op, but to respond with a degree of clarity and quickness. If it simply holds out and continues with no answer to the requests and entreaties of members of that community, many of the benefits will be lost and the opportunity for the Province of Manitoba to meet and plan for a new economic future will also be lost. My intervention this evening is simply to say to the representative of the Minister that it is time to take some action and to make some decisions so that Manitoba can go ahead and do some decent planning for the future of its people.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bernard Valcourt (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: RESEARCH-CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED WINNIPEG MANUFACTURING RESEARCH CENTRE. (B) GOVERNMENT POLICY ON CONSULTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the decision to end the ongoing funding of the Institute for Manufacturing Technology in Manitoba was not an easy one for the Government to take. As with many of the difficult decisions announced on November 8, the Government was merely confronting the unpleasant fact that in the presence of the growing national debt we cannot afford to do everything we would like to do.
The ongoing operating costs associated with the Institute of Manufacturing Technology would have been in excess of $20 million per year. It is clear that the previous Government had not adequately considered this expense when it approved the capital project.
Last November 14, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) asked about the impact of the decision affecting the institute. In response I would point out that it would be difficult for anyone to ascribe credibly a specific impact to the decision. I say this because those involved with the project are still struggling to define the type of research and the kinds of equipment the institute would have. As the Hon. Member will know, the previous Government was criticized by the Wright Task Force, the CMA, the Senate Committee on National Finance and others, for its policies with respect to technology centres, and IMT was often cited specifically as a concern.
It was in this context that the November 8 decision was taken. Nevertheless, the federal Government recognizes the importance of manufacturing technology. It acknowledges the efforts of many well-meaning people associated with IMT.
Adjournment Debate
Thus the Minister is pursuing a number of initiatives aimed at keeping manufacturing technology expertise at NRC.
In addition, construction contracts associated with the project will be honoured, and this will see the building substantially completed. As the Minister said in Winnipeg last November, the building offers considerable potential and the Government is determined to see it put to productive use, notwithstanding the financial constraints facing the country. In this regard the Minister has invited the private sector and the provincial Government to participate in the staffing and the operation of the facility.
This proposal holds tremendous promise. As I mentioned before, the task force on federal policies and programs for technology development, the Senate Committee on Science and Technology and other bodies have stressed the need to increase the linkage between government in-house research activity and the private sector applications of the fruits of this research. The Government believes that the private sector is more likely to take an interest in research and use it if it has a financial interest in the activity. It is for this reason that we are optimistic about the Minister's initiative in relation to the Winnipeg institute.

ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-PROPOSED WEATHER SERVICE INFORMATION CHARGE. (B) METHOD OF IMPLEMENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my reasons for requesting clarification of a question I asked in the House some time ago of the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) are quite simple. I blamed the cuts on the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), but the Minister of the Environment was good enough to stand up in the House last week and say that it was not the Minister of Finance, but she who cut the programs in her Department. Therefore the Minister of the Environment is solely responsible for those cuts that did not make any sense at all.
The Minister announced that she was going to charge Canadians for picking up the telephone and dialing atmospheric environment; charge people for dialing the weather office. She announced at the same time that she would do away with guided tours in national parks. There are going to be self-guided tours, whatever they may be.
When I asked the Minister whether she was going to charge people for telephoning the weather office, she verified that. I then asked about the changing weather patterns in this country, and how they affect the farmers of western Canada, fishermen in eastern Canada, the travelling public on our highways in the north and in other parts of Canada. With our ever changing weather conditions they need frequent updates other than just those available from the media. The Minister said in cases of health and safety they will not be charged. In response to a direct question her words were that fishermen would not be charged.

January 28, 1985
Adjournment Debate
The Minister was really on the spot then. How do you determine who is to be charged, and who will make that judgment? Bell Canada will not be a collection agency for the Government of Canada, collecting money for telephone calls, using some kind of a means test. Obviously the employees in the weather office cannot question every caller. If they did it would take time, and even then how could they verify the information. What is a legitimate call? Will they check the social insurance number of every caller to determine whether he is a fisherman, farmer of someone travelling on the highway? How can that be verified?
In announcing these ill-advised cuts the Minister reversed some of her decisions. For example, she reversed the decision on the study of the effect of toxic substances on Herring-gull eggs. That and various other programs in that area will now be continued. I do not want the Minister to reverse this decision the way she reversed that decision. She re-instituted a one person year to carry out the program of all of these people who were cut in the Canadian Wildlife Service. Let the Minister try and deny that. She cannot.
The Minister made a statement to the media today that she would phase in the program on the herring-gull eggs on April 1. That is rather confusing because the cuts were not supposed to take effect until April 1. I do not want the Minister to state here today that she is going to reverse the decision to charge people for telephoning the weather office in the way she made the reversals on the other cuts that she announced. That does not mean anything.
1 want the Minister to explain how she will carry out this policy of charging Canadians for phoning the local weather office. How will the interpretation process of whether health and safety is involved be handled? I feel quite confident that she will stand and say they are really not going to charge for that, or that everybody who phones the weather office will be charged, thereby going back on the statement she made in the House during Question Period. It has to be one way or the other. It cannot be as she stated publicly in this House because that is unworkable. I am very interested to hear what the Minister has to say, and I am very pleased that she attends the late show. I look forward to her retracting that charge on the Canadian public.

speakeroldname: Hon. Suzanne Blais-Grenier (Minister of the Environment):
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-PROPOSED WEATHER SERVICE INFORMATION CHARGE. (B) METHOD OF IMPLEMENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my obliging colleague for giving me this opportunity to outline in this House the measures we will be taking to get the funds that will help us complement our weather services. You have noticed that my colleague, who had very kind remarks for me before Christmas, has been all smiles when asking his question, even though his tone of voice was outrageously shocked. I remember only the smile.
Mr. Speaker, weather information provided to the general public and to special user groups such as farmers and fishermen is already available through the media, and especially the
electronic press, that is radio, TV and cable television. Maritime weather forecasts for instance, including warnings, are available through the Canadian Coast Guard's marine bands which continuously broadcast them. Thus are categorized the various user groups.
Environment Canada has established radio stations which broadcast weather information 24 hours a day over a special frequency from the 13 most important centres in this country. In the four Atlantic Provinces, provincial governments cooperate financially with us in making this service available to a greater number of users through automatic answering service. This is to reassure my colleague and suggest to him that general weather information is available, through one or the other of those means, to the vast majority of Canadians.
But there are also people who sometimes want additional information, for instance statistics on past weather conditions, weather conditions in other areas of the country or abroad, more specific details on forecasts, or who simply find it more convenient to get such information over the telephone. Because of their limited or specialized scope, such services should not be paid by all Canadians, because they are now paid for out of public funds. People requesting such additional services from now on will have to pay a small fee to get them. This is only fair in my view. For the first year starting in 1985, we expect to collect $1.3 million in this way.
A task force has been set up within the Department to decide on program conditions and determine the services the Government will continue to provide to the media for distribution to the public, as has been done during the past 100 years. Special attention will be paid to maintaining the quality of the weather information services and the implementation of a system of fees that will be realistic, efficient and compensatory-

STATUS OF WOMEN-GOVERNMENT POSITION (B) ELECTION CAMPAIGN STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if we are to believe the Minister of Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier), the government's financial burden has hit Canada's environment the hardest. How incredible!
Mr. Speaker, I think I will go on to another issue and a question which I raised with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) almost two months ago. Hon. Members and Canadians generally are well aware of the promises made by our Prime Minister during the historic debate on women's issue which was seen by TV viewers in Quebec and in the rest of Canada, in fact all Canadian saw it. In the course of that debate with the three party leaders, our Prime Minister made some promises to Canadian women, promises which indeed had to do with the question of equal pay for equal work, and yet this Government, which has now been in office for about five months, has not done anything for Canadian women-all we
January 28, 1985

have heard so far were the empty words uttered by the Prime Minister. He fancies himself as an actor or a comedian, a kind of Johnny Carson who does not really want to respond to the Canadian people, especially not to the women of Canada whose economic needs are so real.
When the issue of equal pay for equal work is raised, Mr. Speaker, one thinks immediately in terms of the 10 per cent of the Canadian labour force which comes under federal jurisdiction. A simple glance at the Canadian banking scene reveals that women workers, particularly at the federal and provincial levels, earn roughly 60 cents for every $1 earned by male workers.
The Government, the Minister and the Prime Minister did promise Canadian women that, the minute they got elected, they would do something right then and there to settle that problem.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made promises to the women of Canada promises upon which the election campaign was built. He told the women of Canada that the moment he was elected tens upon thousands of jobs would be created for Canadians and that the women of Canada would see not only a fair application of equal pay for work of equal value, but that they would also see contract compliance at the federal level, and that people who wanted to do business with the Government would have to toe the line. During the debate last August he said, "J'irai plus loin".
We can see-as we saw in the white paper tabled today which considers the removal of universality of benefits to families who earn $28,000 or more a year-that it is just another shallow promise by a shallow Prime Minister and a shallow Government which have no intention of delivering on the promises made to the women of Canada.
All partisan politics aside, the women of Canada showed during the constitutional debate in 1982 that they would not take a second stage or a second seat to anyone. The women rallied on all political sides-Liberals, Conservatives, New Democrats and non-partisans-to ensure that the women of Canada were given equal rights under the Constitution, against the thrashings, groanings and moanings of the premiers of the Progressive Conservative persuasion in Canada. The women of Canada will not be silent. They are looking at this Government. They are judging the Prime Minister, not on the basis of his verbiage, of which there is plenty, but on the basis of his action.
If we look at the economic results which have occurred since September 4, the political results, and the unfulfilled promises made to the women of Canada, it is clear that this is a Government with a Prime Minister who had no intention of
Adjournment Debate
keeping the promises, who did not deserve the trust of Canadian women or the vote of the Canadian people, and who will be roundly chastised by the voters when they have an opportunity to return a Liberal Government. A Liberal Government will deliver on its promises in a way which the Conservatives have shown they are unable and unwilling to do. The women of Canada will wait four years and will continue to fight for the equality which has been denied them by the Government and the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister has not even bothered to show up in the House for this very important issue.

It is a fact that the principle of equal pay for work of equal value is essential for women to gain economic equality. As the Hon. Member is aware, two departments and one agency-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member should know, two departments and one government agency are responsible for applying the principle of equal pay for work of equal value within the Public Service. First of all, as the employer for the whole Public Service, the Treasury Board has the overall responsibility of determining rates of pay. The Department of Labour keeps employers informed about government policies and encourages them to recognize the problems which can exist in the workplace and to find mutually agreeable solutions. Finally, the Canadian Human Rights Commission receives the complaints lodged by employees coming under federal jurisdiction who were unable to obtain satisfaction from their employers.
I wish to emphasize that, to this date, four types of complaints laid by members of the Public Service have been settled to their satisfaction. The employees involved were able to obtain a satisfactory settlement in every case. It is only recently that one case had to be referred to a panel of the Human Rights Commission.
Legislation guaranteeing equal pay for work of equal value has existed since 1977. However, these measures by themselves are not enough. They have to be applied efficiently. In the Speech from the Throne we find a commitment by the new Government guaranteeing compliance with the principle or equal pay in all sectors under federal jurisdiction. The Minis-

January 28, 1985

ter responsible for the Status of Women has already written to his colleagues, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight), with a view to initiating discussions to ensure that Canadian women will achieve economic equality in the workplace. This will happen eventually and as soon as possible.
